q: A company runs an application on Amazon EC2 instances in Account A. The application must read items from an Amazon DynamoDB table that lives in Account B. The security team prohibits long-term credentials on instances.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an IAM user in Account B with read access to the table. Store the user's access keys in environment variables on the EC2 instances.
Create an IAM role in Account B with read access to the table and a trust policy that allows the EC2 instance role in Account A to assume it. Grant the instance role sts:AssumeRole on that role.
Create a service control policy (SCP) in AWS Organizations that grants Account A read access to the table in Account B.
Export the DynamoDB table to Amazon S3 every night and import it into a new table in Account A.
q.k: cross-account + no long-term credentials → role in the target account + sts:AssumeRole
x: Works, but these are long-term credentials on the instance, which is exactly what the scenario forbids.
Standard cross-account pattern: the role lives in the resource's account, its trust policy trusts the source account's role, and the source account needs sts:AssumeRole. Credentials are temporary.
SCPs never grant permissions; they only cap what can be granted.
Adds data staleness (daily copy) and operational overhead, and it isn't access to the original resource.

q: A developer has an IAM identity policy that allows s3:* on the bucket 'reports-prod'. The bucket policy contains a statement that denies all S3 actions when the request does not come through a specific VPC endpoint (aws:SourceVpce). The developer tries to upload a file from a laptop and receives AccessDenied.
What explains this behavior?
o: Bucket policies always take precedence over identity-based policies.
S3 Block Public Access is blocking uploads from the internet.
An explicit Deny in any applicable policy overrides any Allow.
The developer needs an object ACL that grants WRITE permission.
q.k: an explicit Deny always wins
x: There is no precedence between policy types: all of them are evaluated together. If the bucket policy only had Allows, the identity policy would be enough.
Block Public Access applies to public access (policies or ACLs that grant everyone), not to an authenticated user in the same account.
IAM evaluation logic: explicit deny > explicit allow > implicit deny. The request from the laptop doesn't come through the endpoint, so the Deny applies.
ACLs can't override an explicit Deny, and ACLs are disabled on new buckets.

q: A company uses AWS Organizations with 30 member accounts. The security team must guarantee that nobody in any member account, including administrators, can stop or delete AWS CloudTrail trails. The security tooling account must be exempt.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Attach an IAM policy that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail to every IAM user and role in each account.
Create an AWS Config rule that detects stopped trails and triggers automatic remediation to restart logging.
Attach a permissions boundary that denies CloudTrail changes to every administrator role.
Create an SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail and attach it to the OUs that contain the member accounts, keeping the security account in a separate OU.
q.k: 'nobody, including administrators' across many accounts → SCP (preventive, central)
x: An account administrator can remove that policy, and it has to be maintained on every identity.
Detective, not preventive: the trail would be stopped for a while. More moving parts.
Same as A: it must be applied to every role, and an admin with IAM permissions could bypass it.
SCPs restrict every principal in member accounts (including root) and are managed in one place. The exemption comes from the OU structure.

q: An SCP that denies ec2:RunInstances outside eu-west-1 is attached to the root of an organization. Users in member accounts are correctly blocked, but administrators in the management account can still launch instances in us-east-1.
Why?
o: SCPs do not affect users or roles in the management account.
SCPs take up to 24 hours to propagate to all accounts.
The management account administrators use the root user, which is never affected by SCPs.
SCPs attached to the organization root only apply to new accounts.
q.k: SCPs don't apply to the management account
x: Correct: SCPs never restrict the management account. That's why you shouldn't run workloads in it.
SCPs take effect almost immediately.
The root user of member accounts IS affected by SCPs. The reason here is that this is the management account.
They apply to every account under the root, existing and new.

q: For data residency reasons, a company must ensure that no resources are created outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 in any of its 50 AWS accounts. Global services such as IAM, Route 53, and CloudFront must keep working.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Disable all other AWS Regions in the account settings of each account.
Create an SCP that denies all actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-west-1 or eu-central-1, excluding global services with NotAction, and attach it to the organization's OUs.
Deploy an AWS Config rule in every Region that flags resources created outside the allowed Regions.
Attach a permissions boundary to every IAM role that restricts actions to the two Regions.
q.k: Region restriction at scale → SCP with aws:RequestedRegion (+ exceptions for global services)
x: Only opt-in Regions can be disabled; Regions enabled by default can't.
The documented pattern: Deny with an aws:RequestedRegion condition and NotAction for global services, applied centrally.
Detects but doesn't prevent. The requirement is 'ensure no resources are created'.
Must be applied to every role and doesn't cover new roles created without a boundary.

q: A platform team wants to let developers create IAM roles for their own AWS Lambda functions. The team must prevent developers from creating roles with more permissions than the developers themselves are allowed to have (privilege escalation).
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Grant developers IAMFullAccess and review AWS CloudTrail logs weekly for suspicious role creations.
Have the platform team create every role on request through a ticketing system.
Define a permissions boundary policy and allow developers to create roles only if the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition requires that boundary to be attached.
Attach an SCP to the account that denies iam:CreateRole.
q.k: delegate role creation without privilege escalation → permissions boundary
x: After-the-fact review: the escalation would already have happened.
Works but delegates nothing; high overhead and a bottleneck.
Permissions boundaries set the maximum effective permissions of a role. With the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition, developers can only create 'contained' roles.
Blocks role creation entirely, which contradicts the requirement.

q: An application running on Amazon EC2 needs to write objects to an S3 bucket in the same account.
What is the MOST secure way to provide credentials to the application?
o: Create an IAM role with the required S3 permissions and attach it to the instance through an instance profile.
Create an IAM user, generate access keys, and pass them to the instance through user data.
Store IAM user access keys in AWS Secrets Manager and rotate them every 30 days.
Bake IAM user access keys into the AMI used by the Auto Scaling group.
q.k: credentials for EC2 → instance profile (role), never access keys
x: The role delivers temporary credentials that rotate automatically through instance metadata. Recommended practice.
User data is readable from the instance and the console, and these are long-term keys.
Better than C, but still long-term keys to manage. Unnecessary when roles exist.
Anyone with access to the AMI gets the keys.

q: A company has 40 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations. Employees already authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID. The company wants employees to sign in once and access the accounts they need, with permissions managed centrally and users provisioned automatically.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create IAM users for each employee in each account and enforce MFA.
Configure Amazon Cognito user pools with Entra ID as a SAML identity provider.
Deploy AWS Directory Service AD Connector in every account.
Enable AWS IAM Identity Center, connect Entra ID as the external identity provider with SAML and SCIM, and assign permission sets to groups per account.
q.k: workforce + many accounts + corporate IdP → IAM Identity Center
x: Thousands of duplicated users, no SSO, no central management.
Cognito is for application users (customers), not for employee access to AWS accounts.
AD Connector is for Active Directory, not native Entra ID, and deploying it in every account doesn't give multi-account SSO.
Identity Center is the service for employee SSO across Organizations. SAML for authentication, SCIM for provisioning users and groups, permission sets for permissions.

q: A mobile app lets customers sign in with Google or Apple accounts. After signing in, each customer must upload photos directly to an S3 bucket, into a prefix that only that customer can access. The company does not want to run a backend for this.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an IAM user for each customer and embed the access keys in the app after sign-in.
Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool federated with the social providers. Grant the authenticated role an S3 policy scoped with the ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} policy variable.
Use IAM Identity Center with Google as an external identity provider.
Make the bucket public with a bucket policy that allows PutObject for all principals.
q.k: app users + temporary AWS credentials → Cognito identity pool + policy variables
x: 5,000 IAM users per account limit and long-term keys on a phone.
The identity pool exchanges the social token for temporary credentials. The policy variable limits each user to their own prefix.
Identity Center is for employees (workforce), not app customers.
Anyone could upload anything to any prefix.

q: A company hires a third-party monitoring SaaS that needs read-only access to the company's AWS account. The vendor serves thousands of customers from its own AWS account.
Which approach provides access while protecting against the confused deputy problem?
o: Create an IAM user for the vendor and share access keys over an encrypted channel.
Create an IAM role that trusts the vendor's account without any conditions.
Create an IAM role that trusts the vendor's AWS account and requires a unique sts:ExternalId provided by the vendor.
Add the vendor's account root user to the company's administrators group.
q.k: third party accessing your account → role + external ID
x: Long-term keys in a third party's hands.
Another customer of the vendor could make the SaaS assume your role (confused deputy).
A unique external ID per customer ensures the vendor only assumes your role when acting on your behalf.
IAM groups can't contain principals from other accounts, and this would grant admin.

q: A company has just created a standalone AWS account (not part of an organization). The security team wants to protect the root user.
Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
o: Enable MFA for the root user.
Create access keys for the root user and store them in AWS Secrets Manager.
Do not create (or delete existing) access keys for the root user.
Use the root user for daily administration but enable AWS CloudTrail.
Attach an SCP that restricts the root user.
q.k: root: MFA + no access keys + not used day to day
x: Essential: MFA on the root user.
The root user shouldn't have access keys anywhere.
No root keys removes the most dangerous vector for programmatic abuse.
The root user shouldn't be used for daily tasks; least-privilege identities exist for that.
SCPs only exist inside Organizations, and this account is standalone.

q: A security team must identify every S3 bucket, KMS key, and IAM role in the organization that can be accessed by principals outside the organization.
Which service should the team use?
o: IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust
q.k: 'accessible by external principals' → IAM Access Analyzer
x: GuardDuty detects threats from logs (anomalous activity); it doesn't analyze resource policies.
Access Analyzer reasons over resource policies and creates findings when they grant access outside the zone of trust (account or organization).
Trusted Advisor has limited checks (such as open buckets) and doesn't cover roles or KMS keys this way.
Inspector scans EC2, ECR, and Lambda for software vulnerabilities.

q: An IAM role used by a batch application has broad permissions that were granted during development. The company wants to reduce the role to only the actions it actually used during the last 90 days.
Which solution requires the LEAST effort?
o: Query AWS CloudTrail logs with Amazon Athena and manually write a new policy.
Use IAM Access Analyzer policy generation based on the role's CloudTrail activity.
Run AWS Trusted Advisor and apply its recommendations.
Enable AWS Config and create a custom rule for the role.
q.k: generate a least-privilege policy from real usage → Access Analyzer policy generation
x: Works, but it's exactly the manual work the service automates.
Access Analyzer reviews CloudTrail and generates a policy with the actions and services used, which you can then refine.
Trusted Advisor doesn't generate IAM policies from activity.
Config evaluates configuration; it doesn't infer the permissions that were used.

q: A bucket in Account B has a bucket policy that allows s3:GetObject for the principal arn:aws:iam::<AccountA>:root. A user in Account A still receives AccessDenied when reading objects.
What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The bucket must have S3 Cross-Region Replication enabled to share objects.
The objects must be made public.
Cross-account access to S3 requires AWS RAM.
The user in Account A does not have an identity-based policy that allows s3:GetObject on the bucket.
q.k: cross-account needs BOTH sides (resource policy + identity policy)
x: Replication has nothing to do with permissions.
Making them public would be a security failure, and it isn't needed.
RAM doesn't share S3 buckets.
Granting Account A in the bucket policy delegates to A's administrator. The user still needs their own IAM Allow.

q: A partner account uploads files into an older S3 bucket owned by the company. The bucket still has ACLs enabled. The company cannot read some of the uploaded objects, because the partner account owns them.
Which solution fixes this with the LEAST operational effort and without depending on the uploader's behavior?
o: Set S3 Object Ownership on the bucket to 'Bucket owner enforced'.
Ask the partner to add the bucket-owner-full-control ACL on every upload.
Ask the partner to make every object public-read.
Replicate the bucket to a new bucket every hour.
q.k: objects from another account unreadable → Object Ownership 'Bucket owner enforced' (ACLs disabled)
x: With this setting ACLs are disabled and the bucket owner owns every object. It's the default on new buckets.
Would work, but depends on the partner always doing it right.
Exposes data publicly.
Cost and complexity, and it doesn't fix object ownership.

q: A company has 12 AWS accounts with separate bills. Finance wants a single bill, wants to benefit from volume pricing tiers across accounts, and wants Savings Plans bought in one account to apply to usage in the others.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an AWS Budget in each account.
Create AWS Organizations and invite all accounts to use consolidated billing.
Enable Cost Explorer in each account and export the data to a shared S3 bucket.
Create cross-account IAM roles so that finance can view each bill.
q.k: one bill + volume discounts + shared Savings Plans → Organizations (consolidated billing)
x: Budgets alert, but they don't consolidate bills or share discounts.
Consolidated billing aggregates usage for pricing tiers and shares RIs and Savings Plans across accounts (by default).
Visibility, not consolidation or discounts.
Only gives read access; it doesn't change billing.

q: A company is starting with AWS and wants a well-architected multi-account environment in a few days: a central log archive account, an audit account, preventive and detective guardrails, and a self-service way to create new accounts that follow the baseline.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Create AWS Organizations manually and write CloudFormation StackSets for every baseline control.
Use AWS Service Catalog to create accounts.
Set up AWS Control Tower and use Account Factory to create new accounts.
Deploy AWS Config conformance packs in a single account.
q.k: fast multi-account landing zone + guardrails + account vending → Control Tower
x: Possible, but it means building by hand what Control Tower already provides.
Service Catalog is a piece that Account Factory uses, but it doesn't build the landing zone or guardrails.
Control Tower creates the landing zone (Log Archive, Audit), applies controls (SCPs + Config), and offers Account Factory.
A single account isn't a multi-account environment, and it only covers the detective part.

q: Developers from several projects share one AWS account. Every EC2 instance is tagged with Project. Each developer's IAM role is tagged with the same Project key. Developers must be able to stop and start only the instances of their own project, including instances created in the future.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST ongoing maintenance?
o: Write an IAM policy per project that lists the instance IDs of that project.
Allow ec2:StartInstances and ec2:StopInstances with the condition that aws:ResourceTag/Project equals ${aws:PrincipalTag/Project}.
Move every project to its own AWS account.
Use AWS Resource Groups to group instances by project.
q.k: tag-based permissions that scale on their own → ABAC (ResourceTag = PrincipalTag)
x: The policy must be updated for every new instance.
ABAC: one policy compares the resource tag with the principal tag. New instances are covered without changes.
Valid long term, but a huge migration for this requirement.
Resource Groups organizes resources but doesn't grant or restrict permissions.

q: Administrators can terminate production EC2 instances. The company wants terminations to be allowed only when the administrator signed in with MFA.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Enable MFA on the root user.
Add a Deny for ec2:TerminateInstances when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false (BoolIfExists) to the administrators' policy.
Enable termination protection on all instances.
Create a CloudTrail alert for every TerminateInstances call.
q.k: require MFA for specific actions → aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent condition
x: The root user isn't the one performing the operation.
The MFA condition key in the policy applies the rule to exactly that action.
Prevents termination entirely (even with MFA), and it can be disabled.
Detects afterwards; it doesn't prevent.

q: An S3 bucket must trigger an AWS Lambda function whenever a new object is created. When the event notification is configured, the invocation fails due to missing permissions.
Which policy must grant Amazon S3 permission to invoke the function?
o: The Lambda function's resource-based policy, allowing the s3.amazonaws.com principal with the bucket ARN as the source.
q.k: who can invoke the Lambda → the function's resource-based policy
x: The execution role defines what the function can do, not who can invoke it.
The bucket policy controls access to the bucket, not to the function.
Correct: lambda:AddPermission with the s3.amazonaws.com principal and SourceArn/SourceAccount to avoid the confused deputy problem.
SCPs don't grant permissions.

q: Servers in a company's data center must call AWS APIs. The security team forbids long-term access keys. The company runs its own PKI and every server has an X.509 certificate.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an IAM user per server and rotate the keys every 7 days.
Use an Amazon Cognito identity pool.
Use AWS IAM Identity Center with the corporate directory.
Use IAM Roles Anywhere with the company's certificate authority as a trust anchor.
q.k: servers outside AWS + X.509 certificates → IAM Roles Anywhere
x: Still long-term keys.
Cognito is for end users of apps.
Identity Center is for people, not workloads.
Roles Anywhere exchanges an X.509 certificate from your CA for temporary IAM role credentials.

q: A company runs Windows workloads on Amazon EC2 that must join the existing on-premises Active Directory domain. Policy forbids storing or caching directory data in the cloud. Authentication requests must go to the on-premises domain controllers.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with a two-way forest trust
q.k: 'no directory caching in the cloud', redirect to on-prem AD → AD Connector
x: AD Connector is a proxy: it forwards requests to the on-premises AD without storing directory data in AWS.
Creates a real directory in AWS with its own data, which contradicts the requirement.
Simple AD is a standalone directory (Samba); it doesn't connect to the existing AD.
Doesn't provide domain join for Windows servers.

q: A company runs directory-aware applications on AWS. Authentication must keep working even if the network link to the on-premises data center fails. Users from the on-premises Active Directory must still be able to access the AWS applications.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: AD Connector pointing to the on-premises domain controllers.
AWS Managed Microsoft AD in AWS with a trust relationship to the on-premises AD.
Simple AD synchronized nightly with the on-premises AD.
IAM users created from an export of the on-premises AD.
q.k: AD that survives a link failure + on-prem users → Managed Microsoft AD + trust
x: If the link fails, AD Connector can't authenticate anyone.
The directory lives in AWS (multi-AZ) and keeps working without the link. The trust lets on-premises users access the apps.
Simple AD doesn't support trusts or synchronization with AD.
Not a directory; directory-aware applications can't use it.

q: An account belongs to an OU whose only SCP allows s3:* and ec2:* (the default FullAWSAccess policy has been removed). An IAM user in that account has an identity policy that allows dynamodb:*.
What can the user do with DynamoDB?
o: Everything, because the identity policy explicitly allows it.
Nothing, because DynamoDB actions are not allowed by the SCP.
Everything, unless a permissions boundary is attached.
q.k: effective permissions = intersection (SCP ∩ identity ∩ boundary…)
x: The IAM Allow only takes effect if the SCP also allows it.
No rule grants read-only here.
SCPs set the maximum. Since DynamoDB isn't included, no identity policy can grant it.
The boundary also restricts, but the SCP already blocks.

q: An access key for an IAM user was accidentally committed to a public Git repository.
What should the company do FIRST?
o: Remove the commit from the repository history.
Deactivate the access key, then create a new key and rotate it in the applications.
q.k: leaked key → deactivate it immediately
x: The key is already public and may have been copied.
Useful to detect abuse, but it doesn't cut off access.
Doesn't invalidate the key, which may already have been copied.
First invalidate the exposed credential; then investigate its use with CloudTrail.

q: A security team suspects that temporary credentials of an EC2 instance role were exfiltrated. The role is used by a production fleet. The team must invalidate all credentials issued so far with minimal disruption and without deleting the role.
What should the team do?
o: Use 'Revoke active sessions' on the role, which adds a policy that denies access to tokens issued before the current time.
Detach and re-attach the instance profile on every instance.
q.k: invalidate temporary credentials already issued → revoke active sessions (aws:TokenIssueTime)
x: The trust policy controls who can assume the role from now on; credentials already issued remain valid.
Adds a Deny conditioned on aws:TokenIssueTime. Legitimate instances get new credentials automatically.
Doesn't invalidate the stolen credentials.
Irrelevant to role credentials.

q: A web application uses Amazon API Gateway REST APIs. Only users who have signed up and signed in through the application should be able to call the APIs. The company wants a managed user directory with sign-up, sign-in, and MFA.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Use an Amazon Cognito user pool and configure a Cognito user pool authorizer on the API.
Create an IAM user for every application user and use IAM authorization.
Use AWS IAM Identity Center for application users.
Add a resource policy to the API that allows the company's IP range.
q.k: app user directory + API Gateway → Cognito user pool authorizer
x: The user pool handles sign-up, sign-in, and MFA and issues JWTs that API Gateway validates natively.
Doesn't scale and is the wrong tool for end users.
Identity Center is for internal staff.
Restricting by IP doesn't authenticate users.

q: A company wants every account in its organization, including accounts created in the future, to be able to read objects from a central S3 bucket that holds shared software packages.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Add each account ID to the bucket policy and update it when accounts are created.
Share the bucket through AWS RAM.
Add a bucket policy statement that allows s3:GetObject when aws:PrincipalOrgID equals the organization ID.
Make the bucket public and block other organizations with an SCP.
q.k: 'every account in the org' in a resource policy → aws:PrincipalOrgID
x: Works, but must be maintained by hand.
RAM doesn't share S3 buckets.
A single condition covers every current and future account.
SCPs don't control principals of other organizations; public means public.

q: A company must record API activity from all accounts in its organization, including accounts added later, into a single S3 bucket in a log archive account. Member accounts must not be able to disable this logging.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create a trail in each account with CloudFormation StackSets.
Create an organization trail from the management account (or a delegated administrator) and deliver logs to the central bucket.
q.k: CloudTrail for the whole organization → organization trail
x: Works, but each account could modify its trail, and there are more pieces to maintain.
An organization trail applies automatically to every account, and member accounts can't modify or delete it.
Config records configuration changes, not API activity.
It's for application metrics and logs, not API auditing.

q: A web application on EC2 has a server-side request forgery (SSRF) vulnerability. The security team worries that an attacker could use it to read the instance role credentials from the instance metadata service.
Which action BEST mitigates this risk?
o: Add a security group rule that denies traffic to 169.254.169.254.
Encrypt the EBS volumes with AWS KMS.
Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens = required) on the instances.
Move the instances to a private subnet.
q.k: protect role credentials from SSRF → require IMDSv2
x: Security groups don't filter traffic to the instance metadata service and have no deny rules.
Unrelated to metadata access.
IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained with a PUT and headers, which a typical SSRF (GET) can't get.
The metadata service is local to the instance; the subnet doesn't matter.

q: An Amazon ECS task running on AWS Fargate must read objects from an S3 bucket. The task already pulls its image from Amazon ECR and sends logs to CloudWatch Logs.
Where should the S3 read permissions be granted?
o: In the container instance IAM role.
q.k: permissions YOUR code uses in ECS → task role; the agent (pull/logs) → execution role
x: The execution role is used by the ECS agent to pull the image and send logs, not by your application.
The task role delivers credentials to the task's containers. That's where S3 access goes.
With Fargate there are no container instances to manage.
Controls who can access the repository, not S3.

q: A company uses IAM Identity Center. The Developers group needs administrator access in the three development accounts and read-only access in the production account.
How should this be configured?
o: Create IAM users in each account and add them to local groups.
Create an SCP that grants administrator access to the development OU.
Create two permission sets (AdministratorAccess and ReadOnlyAccess) and assign them to the Developers group in the corresponding accounts.
Create one Cognito group per environment.
q.k: Identity Center: permission set + group + account
x: You lose SSO and central management.
SCPs don't grant permissions.
An assignment is group × permission set × account. Identity Center creates the required roles in each account.
Cognito doesn't manage access to AWS accounts.

q: An administrator of a member account could remove the account from the organization and escape all SCP guardrails.
How can the company prevent this?
o: Attach an SCP that denies organizations:LeaveOrganization.
Enable AWS CloudTrail in the account.
q.k: prevent leaving the organization → SCP denying LeaveOrganization
x: A standard SCP in any landing zone.
They can still use the API.
Only records what happened.
Not the way to control this.

q: A data science team needs temporary access to a production S3 bucket. The security team requires that all access be done through roles with credentials that expire automatically, and that each access be attributable to the individual person in CloudTrail.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Share one IAM user among the team with MFA enabled.
Let each person assume a role with a short maximum session duration and require a source identity (sts:SourceIdentity) that is set to the person's username.
Create a role with no session limit and share its ARN.
Create access keys for each person and delete them after the project.
q.k: attribute actions to a person through roles → source identity
x: Shared credentials make attribution impossible.
Credentials expire with the session duration. The source identity travels with the session (even through role chaining) and is logged in CloudTrail.
The maximum session duration is at most 12 hours, and this doesn't solve attribution.
Long-term keys, not temporary.

q: A company with 20 accounts in AWS Organizations bought Savings Plans in its production account. Finance notices that the discount is also being applied to usage in development accounts, and wants the discount to stay only in the production account.
What should the company do?
o: Move the development accounts to a separate OU.
Turn off Savings Plans and RI discount sharing for the production account in the management account's billing preferences.
Attach an SCP that denies Savings Plans usage in development accounts.
Create a separate Savings Plan in each development account.
q.k: control where commitments apply → billing preference: discount sharing
x: OUs don't affect billing discount sharing.
Discount sharing is on by default in consolidated billing; the management account can turn it off per account so the benefit stays in the buying account.
SCPs don't control billing benefits.
Adds cost and doesn't stop the sharing.

q: A company uses IAM Identity Center with an external IdP. If the IdP has an outage, administrators must still be able to access the AWS accounts to handle an incident.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Create a break-glass IAM user (or root access procedure) per critical account with MFA, stored credentials in a secure vault, monitored with alerts on use.
Disable MFA so access is faster during outages.
Share one administrator password among the team.
Rely on Identity Center's built-in directory cache.
q.k: IdP outage → documented break-glass access with MFA and alerts
x: A tightly controlled emergency identity, with MFA, stored securely and with alerts when used, is the recommended break-glass pattern.
Weakens security.
No accountability, and still an insecure practice.
There is no such cache that bypasses an external IdP outage.

q: A company wants every new AWS account created through Control Tower to have default S3 Block Public Access enabled, GuardDuty enabled, and a standard set of IAM roles, without manual work.
Which approach meets these requirements?
o: Ask account owners to follow a checklist.
Use Control Tower controls plus account customizations (for example Account Factory Customization or Customizations for Control Tower) and delegated administrators for GuardDuty.
Create the resources manually after each account is created.
Use one shared IAM user across accounts.
q.k: baseline every new account automatically → Control Tower controls + customizations
x: Manual and inconsistent.
Controls enforce guardrails, account customizations deploy standard resources, and GuardDuty's delegated administrator auto-enables new accounts.
Doesn't scale.
Insecure and unrelated.

q: A developer accidentally attached the AdministratorAccess policy to a role used by a public-facing Lambda function. The security team wants to be alerted within minutes whenever a policy granting full admin is attached to any role.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Create an EventBridge rule matching CloudTrail AttachRolePolicy events with the AdministratorAccess ARN and send to SNS.
q.k: near real-time alert on an API call → CloudTrail event + EventBridge rule
x: Far too slow.
CloudTrail management events reach EventBridge; a rule can match the API call and parameters and notify via SNS.
Unrelated.
Scans vulnerabilities, not IAM changes.

q: A company wants to centrally prevent anyone outside its organization from accessing its S3 buckets and KMS keys, even if a developer writes an overly permissive resource policy.
Which control fits BEST?
o: A resource control policy (RCP) that denies access when aws:PrincipalOrgID is not the company's organization
q.k: org-wide cap on resource access by outsiders → resource control policy (RCP)
x: RCPs cap permissions on resources in member accounts regardless of who calls, so outside principals are blocked even if a resource policy allows them.
SCPs restrict principals inside your org, not outside callers.
Finds sensitive data; doesn't block access.
Detects external access but doesn't prevent it.

q: An application assumes a role in another account. The security team wants role sessions to last at most 1 hour.
Where is this configured?
o: In the role's maximum session duration setting (and the DurationSeconds requested by the caller)
q.k: limit session length → role maximum session duration
x: The role's max session duration (1–12 h) caps how long credentials last; callers can request less.
SCPs don't set session lengths.
Unrelated.
Applies to console passwords of IAM users.

q: A company keeps all workloads, logs, and security tooling in one AWS account. A misconfiguration in a development stack once deleted production resources.
What should a solutions architect recommend to reduce the blast radius?
o: Separate workloads into multiple accounts (for example prod, dev, security, log archive) in AWS Organizations.
q.k: limit blast radius → multi-account strategy
x: Doesn't isolate resources.
Accounts are the strongest isolation boundary in AWS; Organizations adds central governance and billing.
Tags help organize but don't isolate permissions reliably.
Good practice, but doesn't separate environments.

q: Contractors need access to one S3 prefix for 3 weeks. The company uses IAM Identity Center and wants access to end automatically and be easy to audit.
Which solution is BEST?
o: Create IAM users with access keys and remember to delete them.
Assign the contractors' group a scoped permission set and remove the assignment at the end (or use a temporary elevated access process).
Make the prefix public for 3 weeks.
q.k: temporary human access → Identity Center assignment (time-bound), not IAM users
x: Long-term keys that are easy to forget.
Identity Center gives SSO with temporary credentials and a single place to grant and remove access, all logged.
Unsafe.
Violates security and attribution.

q: A company wants to see what each AWS account in its organization costs without logging in to each one.
Which is the simplest approach?
o: Use Cost Explorer in the management account and group by linked account.
Log in to each account monthly.
Build a custom Lambda billing scraper.
q.k: per-account costs centrally → Cost Explorer in the management (payer) account
x: The management account sees consolidated costs and can group or filter by linked account.
Manual and slow.
Reinvents built-in features.
Logs API calls, not costs.

q: A web application needs users to sign in with their corporate SAML IdP and also with Google, and the backend needs a single JWT format regardless of how users signed in.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: An Amazon Cognito user pool with SAML and Google federation
IAM Identity Center application assignments for all customers
A Lambda authorizer that calls each IdP directly
q.k: several external IdPs, one token format for an app → Cognito user pool federation
x: User pools federate SAML, OIDC and social IdPs and issue their own JWTs, so the backend validates one token type.
Doesn't scale and wrong tool.
Identity Center is for workforce access, not app customers.
Custom code reimplementing what Cognito does.

q: A company needs to share an AWS Transit Gateway and Route 53 Resolver rules owned by its network account with all other accounts in the organization.
Which service should be used?
q.k: share resources across accounts → Resource Access Manager
x: RAM shares supported resources (TGWs, subnets, Resolver rules, etc.) with accounts or the whole organization.
Peering connects VPCs; it doesn't share a TGW.
Roles give access to APIs, not a shared resource usable by other accounts' networks.
Catalog of approved products; not resource sharing.

q: An S3 bucket policy grants s3:GetObject to Principal '*' with no conditions, but S3 Block Public Access is enabled at the account level.
What happens to anonymous requests?
o: They succeed because the bucket policy allows them.
They are blocked, because account-level Block Public Access overrides policies that grant public access.
They succeed only from inside AWS.
q.k: Block Public Access overrides public policies/ACLs
x: Block Public Access wins over the policy.
Account-level BPA prevents public access regardless of bucket policies or ACLs.
No such exception.
No such behavior.

q: A financial services company has 120 AWS accounts in AWS Organizations, grouped into OUs for production, development and sandbox. A recent audit found that developers in sandbox accounts launched GPU instances in Regions where the company has no data processing agreement. The company must prevent any resource creation outside eu-west-1 and eu-central-1 in sandbox and development accounts, while still allowing global services such as IAM and Route 53 to work. Production accounts already have their own controls and must not be affected.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Create an SCP that denies all actions when aws:RequestedRegion is not eu-west-1 or eu-central-1, with a NotAction list for global services, and attach it to the development and sandbox OUs.
Create an IAM policy with the same Region condition and attach it to every IAM role in the development and sandbox accounts by using CloudFormation StackSets.
Enable AWS Config in all Regions of the development and sandbox accounts with a custom rule that terminates resources created outside the approved Regions.
Create an SCP that allows only actions in eu-west-1 and eu-central-1, and attach it to the organization root.
q.k: prevent + many accounts + only some OUs → SCP with aws:RequestedRegion attached to those OUs
x: A deny SCP at the right OUs is preventive, central and leaves production untouched; NotAction keeps global services working.
Policies on every role are hard to keep complete (new roles), and admins could remove them.
Detective and reactive: resources exist until remediation runs, and Config must be enabled everywhere.
Attaching at the root affects production too, and an allow-list SCP without the global services exception would break IAM and Route 53.

q: A company runs a SaaS application in Account A. A customer wants the application to write daily reports into the customer's own S3 bucket in Account B. The customer's security team requires that the application uses temporary credentials, that the objects are owned by the customer, and that the customer can revoke access at any time without involving the SaaS provider.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: The customer creates an IAM user for the SaaS provider and shares the access keys; the customer deletes the user to revoke access.

The customer creates an IAM role in Account B with s3:PutObject on the bucket and a trust policy for the provider's account with an external ID; the bucket uses Object Ownership set to bucket owner enforced. The application assumes the role.
The customer adds a bucket policy that allows s3:PutObject for Account A's root principal; the provider writes with its own role.
The customer shares the bucket with Account A by using AWS RAM.
q.k: temporary creds + customer owns objects + customer revokes → role in customer account (external ID) + bucket owner enforced
x: Long-term keys, which violates the requirement.
The customer controls the role and can delete it or change its trust policy any time; credentials are temporary; bucket owner enforced makes the customer own all objects.

Works for writing, but the customer can only revoke by editing the policy, and objects written by Account A would not be customer-owned unless ownership is enforced; it also doesn't use credentials issued by the customer.
RAM doesn't share S3 buckets.

q: A company has a central security account and 40 workload accounts. The security team must be able to read CloudTrail logs, Config data and GuardDuty findings from all accounts in one place, and workload account administrators must not be able to disable GuardDuty or tamper with the logs.
Which TWO actions should a solutions architect recommend? (Select TWO.)
o: Designate the security account as the delegated administrator for GuardDuty and enable it automatically for all member accounts.
Create an organization trail that delivers logs to an S3 bucket in a log archive account, and protect the bucket with a bucket policy and S3 Object Lock.
Create an IAM user in every workload account for the security team.
Ask workload administrators to forward logs to the security account by email.
Enable GuardDuty separately in each account and give workload admins full GuardDuty permissions.
q.k: central security visibility + tamper-proof → delegated admin + org trail to locked log archive
x: Delegated administration centralizes findings and auto-enables new accounts; members can't disable it.
Org trails can't be changed by member accounts; a separate locked bucket protects the logs.
Doesn't scale and adds long-term credentials.
Not a technical control.
Lets workload admins disable it.

q: Developers use a shared AWS account. Each developer must be able to create Lambda functions and the IAM roles those functions use, but the roles must never be able to access the production DynamoDB tables or modify IAM. The platform team wants to stop approving each role manually.
What should the platform team do?
o: Give developers iam:CreateRole and iam:AttachRolePolicy only when the iam:PermissionsBoundary condition requires a boundary policy that denies production DynamoDB tables and IAM actions.
Give developers AdministratorAccess and audit with CloudTrail.
Attach an SCP to the account denying iam:CreateRole.
Create a single shared role that all Lambda functions must use.
q.k: self-service role creation within limits → permissions boundary enforced on CreateRole
x: Developers can create roles freely, but every role is capped by the boundary, so it can never reach production tables or IAM.
Allows escalation; audit is after the fact.
Stops developers from creating roles at all.
Every function would get the union of all permissions.

q: A company federates its workforce into 25 AWS accounts through IAM Identity Center connected to an external IdP. During last month's IdP outage, nobody could sign in to AWS for 3 hours, and an urgent production fix was delayed.
Which change improves access resilience while keeping security controls?
o: Replace Identity Center with IAM users for everyone.

Create a small number of break-glass IAM users or root credentials for critical accounts, protected with hardware MFA, stored in a sealed vault, with EventBridge alerts whenever they are used, and test the procedure regularly.
Disable MFA on Identity Center so sign-in is faster.
Configure a second Identity Center instance in another Region.
q.k: IdP down → documented, monitored break-glass access
x: Loses central management and adds many long-term credentials.
A tightly controlled emergency path gives access during IdP outages while staying auditable.
Doesn't help when the IdP itself is down, and weakens security.
An organization has a single Identity Center instance; it still depends on the same IdP.

q: A mobile game stores each player's save files in Amazon S3. Players sign in through Amazon Cognito user pools. The game client must upload and download save files directly to S3, and a player must never be able to read another player's files. The company wants no backend servers for this.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Generate presigned URLs from an API backed by EC2.
Use a Cognito identity pool that maps authenticated users to an IAM role whose policy allows s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject only on arn:aws:s3:::bucket/${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub}/*.
Make the bucket public and use random object names.
Create an IAM user per player at sign-up.
q.k: per-user prefix isolation without a backend → identity pool + policy variable
x: Works but adds a backend, which the company doesn't want.
The identity pool gives temporary credentials, and the policy variable confines each player to their own prefix.
Insecure.
IAM user limits and long-term credentials.

q: A security engineer finds that an IAM role used by a CI/CD pipeline has the policy s3:* on *. The pipeline only needs to upload artifacts to one bucket and read from another. The team wants to fix this quickly without breaking the pipeline.
Which approach is BEST?
o: Remove the policy and wait for pipeline failures to identify missing permissions.
Use IAM Access Analyzer to generate a policy from the role's CloudTrail activity over the last 90 days, review it, and replace the broad policy.
Attach an SCP denying s3:* to the account.
q.k: right-size an over-permissive role from real usage → Access Analyzer policy generation
x: Breaks production and is slow.
The generated policy lists only the actions and resources actually used, ready for review.
Breaks everything that uses S3.
Doesn't change permissions.

q: An application in Account A reads secrets from AWS Secrets Manager in Account B. The secret is encrypted with a customer managed KMS key in Account B. The application's role has secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on the secret ARN, and the secret's resource policy allows the role. The call still fails with AccessDenied.
What is the MOST likely missing configuration?
o: The KMS key policy in Account B doesn't allow the role from Account A to use kms:Decrypt (and the role lacks kms:Decrypt on the key).
The secret must be replicated to Account A.
Secrets Manager doesn't support cross-account access.
The secret must be encrypted with the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager.
q.k: cross-account secret + CMK → KMS key policy must allow the other account too
x: Cross-account secret access needs the secret policy, the KMS key policy and the caller's IAM policy to all allow it.
Not required.
It does, with resource policies and a customer managed key.
The AWS managed key can't be used cross-account; the CMK is actually required.

q: A company wants employees to access the AWS Management Console of 30 accounts with their corporate identities. Permissions must differ by team and by environment, and when someone leaves the company, their AWS access must end as soon as they are disabled in the corporate directory.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: IAM Identity Center with the corporate IdP as identity source, automatic provisioning with SCIM, and permission sets assigned to groups per account
An IAM user per employee per account, removed by a nightly script
A Cognito user pool for employees
A shared role per team, with the password rotated monthly
q.k: workforce SSO + immediate deprovisioning → Identity Center + SCIM
x: SCIM keeps users and groups in sync, so disabling someone in the IdP removes access; permission sets map team and environment.
Thousands of users and delayed removal.
Cognito is for customer-facing apps.
Shared credentials and no individual control.

q: A company stores sensitive data in S3 buckets across 50 accounts. It wants to ensure that data can only be accessed by principals in its organization and only from its corporate networks or VPCs, even if someone writes a permissive bucket policy by mistake.
Which approach implements this data perimeter with the LEAST ongoing effort?
o: Add the same conditions to every bucket policy manually.

Use a resource control policy (RCP) that denies S3 access unless aws:PrincipalOrgID matches the organization and the request comes from expected networks (aws:SourceVpc or aws:SourceIp), with exceptions for AWS service principals.
Use Amazon Macie to find public buckets weekly.
q.k: organization-wide data perimeter on resources → RCP
x: Error-prone across many buckets.
RCPs apply centrally to resources in member accounts and override permissive bucket policies.
Detective only.
Unrelated.

q: A development environment runs EC2 instances in private subnets in two Availability Zones. The instances need occasional outbound internet access to download patches. High availability is NOT required for this environment, and the company wants to minimize cost.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
o: Deploy one NAT gateway in each AZ's public subnet and point each private route table to the NAT gateway in its AZ.
Deploy a single NAT gateway in one public subnet and point the route tables of both private subnets to it.
Deploy a NAT gateway in each private subnet.
Attach an egress-only internet gateway and route 0.0.0.0/0 to it.
q.k: 'HA not required' + 'minimize cost' → a single NAT gateway
x: This is the production (HA) design, but it doubles the hourly cost.
One shared NAT gateway is enough when losing internet egress during that AZ's outage is acceptable. Mind the cross-AZ data transfer cost.
A NAT gateway must be in a public subnet (with a route to the IGW) to provide internet egress.
An egress-only IGW only works with IPv6.

q: A production workload runs in private subnets in AZ-a and AZ-b. Both private route tables send 0.0.0.0/0 to a single NAT gateway in AZ-a. During an AZ-a outage, the healthy instances in AZ-b also lost internet access.
How should a solutions architect redesign the network to avoid this?
o: Replace the NAT gateway with a larger NAT instance in AZ-b.
Add a second internet gateway to the VPC.
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each AZ and give each AZ's private subnets a route table that points to the NAT gateway in the same AZ.
Move the instances in AZ-b to public subnets.
q.k: NAT gateways are zonal → one per AZ with per-AZ route tables
x: A single NAT (instance or gateway) is still a single point of failure.
A VPC supports only one internet gateway, and the IGW wasn't the problem.
This isolates failures: each AZ depends only on its own NAT gateway.
Exposes the instances to the internet for no reason.

q: Logs show that a specific IP range is sending malicious requests to web servers in a public subnet. The security team must block that range immediately while keeping the site available to everyone else.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Add an inbound deny rule for the IP range to the web servers' security group.
Remove the route to the internet gateway.
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the subnet.
Add an inbound deny rule for the IP range to the subnet's network ACL, with a rule number lower than the allow rules.
q.k: 'block an IP range' → network ACL (security groups have no deny)
x: Security groups only support allow rules.
Would make the site unreachable for everyone.
Records the traffic but doesn't block it.
NACLs support deny and are evaluated in ascending rule-number order. The deny must come before the general allow.

q: A subnet's custom network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 and outbound TCP 443 to 0.0.0.0/0. Clients can open TCP connections to the HTTPS server in the subnet, but they never receive responses.
What is the cause?
o: Network ACLs are stateless, so outbound traffic to the clients' ephemeral ports (1024-65535) must be allowed.
The security group must explicitly allow outbound TCP 443.
The NACL must also allow inbound ephemeral ports.
HTTPS needs UDP 443 to be allowed.
q.k: NACLs are stateless → allow the ephemeral return ports
x: Responses go to the client's ephemeral port, not port 443. A stateless NACL needs an explicit outbound rule for them.
Security groups are stateful: if inbound is allowed, the response goes out automatically.
Inbound ephemeral ports would be needed for connections the server initiates, not for responses.
HTTPS runs over TCP (except HTTP/3, which isn't the case here).

q: A three-tier application runs web servers in an Auto Scaling group. The application tier must accept traffic on port 8080 only from the web tier. Web instances are replaced frequently and their IP addresses change.
How should the application tier security group be configured?
o: Allow port 8080 from the CIDR blocks of the whole VPC.
Allow port 8080 with the web tier's security group ID as the source.
Allow port 8080 from each web instance's private IP and update the rule with a Lambda function.
Allow port 8080 from 0.0.0.0/0 and block other traffic with a network ACL.
q.k: allow traffic from another tier that scales → reference its security group
x: Works, but is much broader than needed (least privilege).
Referencing the SG allows any instance that has it, regardless of IP.
Fragile and needless overhead.
Opening to 0.0.0.0/0 contradicts the requirement.

q: EC2 instances in private subnets upload several terabytes per day to Amazon S3 buckets in the same Region through a NAT gateway. The NAT gateway data processing charges are high.
Which solution reduces cost the MOST?
o: Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint.
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance.
Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and add it to the private subnets' route tables.
q.k: S3/DynamoDB from the VPC, same Region, cost → gateway endpoint (free)
x: Works, but has hourly and per-GB charges. The gateway endpoint doesn't.
Saves part of the charge, but adds management and a single point of failure; traffic still goes over the internet.
S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints are free and take the traffic off the NAT.
Speeds up long-distance uploads, and costs more.

q: An application runs in private subnets that have no route to the internet, by security policy. The application must read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager and send messages to Amazon SQS.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create gateway VPC endpoints for Secrets Manager and SQS.
Add a NAT gateway and restrict it with security groups.
Create interface VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) for Secrets Manager and SQS with private DNS enabled.
Create a VPC peering connection to the AWS service VPC.
q.k: AWS service (other than S3/DynamoDB) without internet → interface endpoint
x: Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
Means giving internet egress, which the policy forbids.
Interface endpoints put private ENIs in your VPC. With private DNS, the SDK uses the default endpoints with no code changes.
You can't peer with AWS service VPCs.

q: On-premises servers connect to a VPC through AWS Direct Connect with a private virtual interface. The servers must access Amazon S3 privately, without traversing the public internet.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create an S3 gateway endpoint in the VPC and route on-premises traffic through it.
Create an S3 interface endpoint in the VPC and have on-premises clients use its endpoint-specific DNS names.
Create a NAT gateway in the VPC for the on-premises traffic.
q.k: S3 from on-premises over DX/VPN → interface endpoint (gateway endpoints aren't reachable from outside)
x: Gateway endpoints only work from inside the VPC; on-premises traffic can't use them.
The interface endpoint has private IPs reachable over DX/VPN.
A NAT gateway goes out to the public internet.
Uses CloudFront's network over the internet.

q: A company uses an S3 gateway endpoint for its private subnets. Security requirements: (1) instances in the VPC must be able to reach only the company's approved buckets through the endpoint, and (2) a sensitive bucket must reject any request that does not come through that endpoint.
Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
o: Attach an endpoint policy to the gateway endpoint that allows access only to the approved buckets.
Add a bucket policy on the sensitive bucket that denies requests when aws:SourceVpce is not the endpoint ID.
Add a security group to the gateway endpoint.
Enable S3 Block Public Access on all buckets.
Add a NACL rule that denies S3 prefix list traffic.
q.k: endpoint policy (which buckets from the VPC) + bucket policy aws:SourceVpce (where the bucket is accessed from)
x: The endpoint policy filters what can be done through the endpoint.
Restricts the bucket so it can only be accessed through the endpoint.
Gateway endpoints don't support security groups (interface endpoints do).
Blocks public access but doesn't require the endpoint.
Would cut off all traffic to S3.

q: A company has 15 VPCs, and the number grows every quarter. Every VPC must be able to communicate with every other VPC and with the on-premises network through one VPN connection. Peering is becoming unmanageable.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Create a full mesh of VPC peering connections and a VPN connection to each VPC.
Create a transit VPC with EC2-based routers.
Use AWS PrivateLink between all VPCs.
Create an AWS Transit Gateway, attach every VPC, and attach the Site-to-Site VPN to the transit gateway.
q.k: many VPCs + on-prem, hub-and-spoke → Transit Gateway
x: A full mesh grows as n·(n-1)/2 connections, and peering isn't transitive.
The legacy pattern, with instances to manage.
PrivateLink exposes specific services; it doesn't provide full network connectivity.
Transit Gateway is a managed regional router: one attachment per VPC and a single VPN shared by all.

q: VPC A is peered with VPC B, and VPC B is peered with VPC C. Instances in VPC A cannot reach instances in VPC C, even though all route tables point to the peering connections.
Why?
o: VPC peering does not support transitive routing.
Peering connections only work within the same AZ.
Security groups cannot reference peered VPCs.
VPC C must enable DNS resolution.
q.k: peering is not transitive
x: A can't reach C through B. You need an A-C peering or a Transit Gateway.
Peering works across AZs, Regions, and accounts.
They can reference SGs of a peered VPC in the same Region, and anyway that isn't the cause.
DNS doesn't affect routing.

q: After an acquisition, a company needs an application in VPC X to call an internal API in VPC Y. Both VPCs use the CIDR 10.0.0.0/16. Only this API must be reachable, in one direction.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create a VPC peering connection between VPC X and VPC Y.
Expose the API through a Network Load Balancer in VPC Y as a VPC endpoint service, and create an interface endpoint in VPC X.
Attach both VPCs to a transit gateway and propagate routes.
Change VPC X's primary CIDR block.
q.k: overlapping CIDRs + one specific service, one-way → PrivateLink
x: Peering doesn't support overlapping CIDRs.
PrivateLink doesn't route networks: the consumer sees an ENI with an IP from its own VPC. Works with overlapping CIDRs and exposes only that service.
With identical ranges routing is ambiguous; it doesn't work without extra NAT.
A VPC's primary CIDR can't be changed.

q: A SaaS provider wants to offer its service to hundreds of customers who run workloads in their own VPCs. Traffic must stay on the AWS network. Customers must not get network access to the provider's VPC, and the provider must not see the customers' networks.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: VPC peering with every customer VPC.
A transit gateway shared with customers through AWS RAM.
A public Application Load Balancer protected by AWS WAF.
A VPC endpoint service (AWS PrivateLink) backed by a Network Load Balancer, with customers creating interface endpoints.
q.k: SaaS for many VPCs without exposing networks → PrivateLink endpoint service
x: Would give full two-way network connectivity and doesn't scale well to hundreds of customers.
Would connect every customer's network together.
Traffic would go over the public internet.
PrivateLink is one-way and only exposes the service. The provider can approve each connection.

q: A company needs encrypted connectivity between its office and a VPC within two days. Traffic volume is low and some latency variation is acceptable.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Order an AWS Direct Connect dedicated connection.
Set up an AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection to a virtual private gateway or transit gateway.
Use VPC peering with the office network.
Use AWS Client VPN for every office device.
q.k: fast + encrypted + low volume → Site-to-Site VPN
x: Direct Connect takes weeks to provision and isn't encrypted by default.
IPsec VPN is set up in hours, is encrypted, and runs over the internet. Matches the whole scenario.
Peering is VPC-to-VPC only.
Client VPN is for individual users, not for connecting an office network.

q: A company transfers large volumes of data between its data center and AWS and needs consistent, predictable network performance. It also needs a backup path if the primary connection fails, at the lowest possible cost.
Which solution meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively?
o: Use AWS Direct Connect as the primary connection and a Site-to-Site VPN as the backup.
Use two Direct Connect connections at the same location.
Use AWS Direct Connect with no backup, because it has an SLA.
q.k: consistent performance → DX; cheap backup → VPN
x: DX gives predictable latency and bandwidth, and the VPN is an inexpensive backup path that takes over if DX fails.
The VPN runs over the internet: performance isn't predictable.
More expensive, and the shared location is a single point of failure.
A single connection is a single point of failure.

q: A company uses AWS Direct Connect for traffic between its data center and a VPC. A new compliance rule requires all traffic between the sites to be encrypted in transit at the network layer.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Enable encryption on the private virtual interface settings.
Do nothing, because Direct Connect traffic is encrypted by default.
Establish an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect connection.
Use a NAT gateway with TLS termination.
q.k: DX isn't encrypted by default → IPsec VPN over DX (or MACsec on supported dedicated connections)
x: That setting doesn't exist on the VIF.
Direct Connect is a private link, but it isn't encrypted.
IPsec over DX combines the private path with encryption. Some dedicated connections also support MACsec.
A NAT gateway doesn't terminate TLS or encrypt links.

q: A company has one AWS Direct Connect connection in Frankfurt. It needs private connectivity from its data center to VPCs in eu-central-1, eu-west-1, and us-east-1.
Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST effort?
o: Order a Direct Connect connection in each Region.
Create a Direct Connect gateway and associate it with the virtual private gateways (or a transit gateway) of the VPCs in all three Regions.
Create inter-Region VPC peering from eu-central-1 to the other VPCs.
Create Site-to-Site VPNs from Frankfurt to each Region.
q.k: one DX connection → VPCs in several Regions → Direct Connect gateway
x: Expensive and unnecessary.
A Direct Connect gateway is a global resource that connects a VIF to VPCs in any Region.
Peering isn't transitive: on-premises traffic can't pass through the Frankfurt VPC.
Adds complexity and uses the internet as transport.

q: A bank runs critical workloads that depend on AWS Direct Connect and needs maximum resilience against device, connection, and location failures.
Which design meets these requirements?
o: One Direct Connect connection with a Site-to-Site VPN backup.
Two connections on the same device at one Direct Connect location.
Two link aggregation groups (LAGs) at one location.
Separate connections terminating on separate devices in at least two Direct Connect locations.
q.k: 'maximum resilience' for DX → redundant connections in several locations
x: The basic resilience option, but the VPN doesn't match the performance.
If that device or location fails, everything is lost.
A single location is still a point of failure.
AWS's maximum resiliency model: device and location redundancy.

q: An application runs in us-east-1 (primary) and has a standby copy in us-west-2. Users must be routed to us-west-2 only if the primary becomes unhealthy.
Which Amazon Route 53 configuration meets this requirement?
o: Failover routing with a health check on the primary record.
q.k: active-passive → failover routing + health check
x: The primary record with a health check answers while healthy; if it fails, Route 53 returns the secondary.
With weight 0 the secondary never gets traffic unless you change weights manually.
Would send users to the closest Region, not to the primary.
Returns several healthy IPs at once; it isn't active-passive.

q: A company serves a global user base from identical stacks in us-east-1, eu-west-1, and ap-northeast-1. Users must be sent to the Region that gives them the best response time.
Which routing policy should be used?
q.k: 'best response time' → latency-based
x: Routes by the user's location, which doesn't always match the lowest latency.
Route 53 uses latency measurements between networks and AWS Regions to pick the best Region.
Splits proportionally, ignoring latency.
Doesn't choose between Regions.

q: For legal reasons, users located in the EU must always be served by the stack in eu-central-1, and users elsewhere by the stack in us-east-1.
Which routing policy guarantees this?
o: Geolocation routing with an EU record and a default record
q.k: 'must always' by user location (compliance) → geolocation
x: Latency can change and send an EU user to us-east-1.
Splits by percentage, not location.
Geolocation decides based on where the DNS query originates. The default record covers the rest of the world.
Ignores location.

q: A team wants to release a new version of an application gradually: 10% of users go to the new stack and 90% to the current one, and the percentages will be adjusted over several days.
Which Route 53 routing policy should be used?
q.k: traffic percentages (canary/blue-green) → weighted
x: Active-passive; it doesn't split traffic.
Shifts traffic by geographic distance and a bias, not by exact percentages.
Chooses by latency.
You assign weights to each record and Route 53 splits answers in that proportion.

q: A company wants the zone apex example.com to point to its Application Load Balancer.
Which DNS record should be created in Route 53?
o: A CNAME record for example.com pointing to the ALB DNS name.
An A record with the ALB's current IP addresses.
An alias A record for example.com that targets the ALB.
An MX record pointing to the ALB.
q.k: zone apex → alias record
x: DNS doesn't allow a CNAME at the zone apex.
ALB IP addresses change; it would break.
Alias records are a Route 53 extension: they work at the apex, follow IP changes, and queries to AWS resources are free.
MX is for email.

q: A company runs a small fleet of web servers with no load balancer. It wants DNS to return several IP addresses, only of servers that pass health checks, so that clients can choose among them.
Which routing policy meets this requirement?
o: Multivalue answer routing with health checks
q.k: several healthy IPs in the answer, no load balancer → multivalue answer
x: Returns up to 8 healthy records at random. Basic client-side distribution; not a substitute for a load balancer.
Simple routing doesn't support health checks: it would also return failed servers.
Without health checks it can return failed servers.
Only gives a primary and a secondary.

q: A hybrid environment has on-premises DNS servers and a VPC with a Route 53 private hosted zone (aws.corp.internal). On-premises servers must resolve records in the private hosted zone, and EC2 instances must resolve names in the on-premises domain (corp.internal).
Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)
o: Create a Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint and configure on-premises DNS servers to forward aws.corp.internal queries to it.
Create a Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule for corp.internal pointing to the on-premises DNS servers.
Make the private hosted zone public.
Install BIND on an EC2 instance in each subnet.
Associate the private hosted zone with the on-premises network.
q.k: on-prem → AWS = inbound endpoint; AWS → on-prem = outbound endpoint + rule
x: The inbound endpoint receives queries coming from outside the VPC.
The outbound endpoint with a forwarding rule sends queries from the VPC to your on-premises DNS.
Would expose internal names on the internet.
The legacy pattern, with servers to manage.
A private hosted zone can only be associated with VPCs.

q: Administrators currently connect to private EC2 instances through a bastion host with SSH keys. The security team wants to remove the bastion, close all inbound ports, stop managing SSH keys, and log every session.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Move the instances to public subnets with security groups restricted to the office IP range.
Use AWS Systems Manager Session Manager with the SSM Agent and an instance role, and log sessions to S3 or CloudWatch Logs.
Use EC2 Instance Connect through the bastion host.
Use AWS Client VPN and keep the SSH keys.
q.k: no bastion, no inbound ports, no keys, audited sessions → Session Manager
x: Exposes the instances and keeps the keys.
Session Manager uses outbound connections from the agent, authorization goes through IAM, and session logging is built in.
Keeps the bastion and SSH.
Keeps the keys and open ports inside the VPC.

q: Users report intermittent connection failures to an application. A solutions architect needs to find out whether traffic is being rejected by security groups or network ACLs.
Which tool should be used?
q.k: traffic accepted or rejected (ACCEPT/REJECT)? → Flow Logs
x: Copies full packets; too much for this diagnosis.
Records API calls, not network traffic.
Flow Logs record metadata for each flow (IPs, ports, ACCEPT/REJECT).
Analyzes vulnerabilities.

q: A security team must feed the full packet contents of traffic to and from specific EC2 instances into an intrusion detection appliance for deep packet inspection.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: VPC Flow Logs delivered to Amazon S3
VPC Traffic Mirroring with the IDS appliance as the mirror target
q.k: 'packet contents' → Traffic Mirroring
x: Flow Logs don't include packet contents.
Traffic Mirroring copies packets from ENIs to a target (ENI, NLB, or GWLB endpoint) for inspection.
CloudTrail doesn't deal with network traffic.
GuardDuty analyzes flow logs and DNS, but doesn't do deep packet inspection.

q: Workloads in private subnets may only make outbound HTTPS connections to an approved list of domains (for example, *.github.com and api.partner.com). All other outbound traffic must be blocked and logged.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Security groups with outbound rules for the domains.
Network ACLs with the domains' current IP addresses.
AWS WAF attached to the NAT gateway.
AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group, deployed in the egress path.
q.k: egress filtering by domain name → Network Firewall
x: Security groups work with IPs, CIDRs, and SGs, not domains.
IPs change, and NACLs have a limited number of rules.
WAF doesn't attach to a NAT gateway; it protects web apps from inbound traffic.
Network Firewall inspects SNI and Host to filter by domain, and logs the traffic.

q: A company wants to insert a fleet of third-party virtual firewall appliances into the traffic path of its VPCs. The appliances must scale horizontally and be transparent to the applications.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Gateway Load Balancer with the appliances as targets, and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints in the route tables.
Application Load Balancer in front of the appliances.
Network Load Balancer with cross-zone load balancing.
Route 53 weighted routing to the appliances.
q.k: transparent, scalable third-party appliances → Gateway Load Balancer
x: GWLB uses GENEVE to keep the original packet and plugs into route tables through its endpoints.
An ALB terminates HTTP connections; it isn't transparent.
An NLB doesn't insert appliances into the path transparently.
DNS doesn't control the packet path.

q: EC2 instances in a dual-stack subnet must be able to initiate outbound connections to the internet over IPv6. Inbound connections from the internet over IPv6 must be blocked.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: An egress-only internet gateway with a ::/0 route
An internet gateway with a security group that denies inbound IPv6
q.k: IPv6 outbound only → egress-only internet gateway
x: A NAT gateway is for IPv4 (or NAT64), not native IPv6 egress.
The IPv6 equivalent of NAT: allows outbound and blocks connections initiated from outside.
With an IGW the instances are reachable, and SGs have no deny.
It's for VPN and Direct Connect.

q: A solutions architect creates a subnet with the CIDR block 10.0.1.0/27.
How many IP addresses are available for resources in this subnet?
q.k: AWS reserves 5 IPs per subnet
x: That's the whole block; AWS reserves 5 addresses.
The classic calculation (network and broadcast), but AWS reserves 5, not 2.
32 − 5 (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast) = 27.
That would be a /28.

q: A VPC created with 10.0.0.0/24 is running out of IP addresses. The company must add capacity without recreating the VPC or interrupting running workloads.
What should the solutions architect do?
o: Change the VPC's primary CIDR block to 10.0.0.0/16.
Resize the existing subnets to larger CIDR blocks.
Add a secondary IPv4 CIDR block to the VPC and create new subnets in it.
Create a new VPC and peer it with the existing VPC.
q.k: grow a VPC → secondary CIDR
x: The primary CIDR can't be modified.
A subnet's CIDR can't be changed.
A VPC supports secondary CIDR blocks; new subnets are created in them without touching what already runs.
Works, but adds needless complexity.

q: A partner only accepts API calls from IP addresses on its allow list. A company's application runs in private subnets across two AZs in an Auto Scaling group.
How can the company present a small, fixed set of source IP addresses to the partner?
o: Assign an Elastic IP address to each instance at launch.
Route outbound traffic through NAT gateways (one per AZ), each with an Elastic IP, and give the partner those IPs.
Use the VPC CIDR block as the allowed range.
Place an Application Load Balancer in front of the partner API.
q.k: fixed egress IP from private subnets → NAT gateway with an Elastic IP
x: The instances are in private subnets, and EIPs would be lost when instances are replaced.
All outbound traffic uses the NAT gateways' EIPs: a few fixed, stable IPs.
Private IPs; the partner never sees them.
An ALB receives traffic; it doesn't change the source IP of outbound traffic.

q: A company has 20 VPCs attached to one transit gateway. Development VPCs must not communicate with production VPCs, but both must reach a shared-services VPC.
How should this be configured?
o: Create separate transit gateway route tables for dev and prod. Associate each VPC with its environment's table and propagate only the shared-services routes (plus same-environment routes) into each.
Use network ACLs in every VPC to block the other environment's CIDRs.
Create two transit gateways and peer them.
Use security groups that reference VPCs from the other environment.
q.k: segmentation in Transit Gateway → multiple TGW route tables
x: TGW route tables isolate traffic between environments and allow reaching shared services. The standard pattern.
Works, but rules must be maintained in every VPC and it's error-prone.
More cost and complexity for something route tables solve.
SGs can't reference SGs across a TGW (only across peering or a shared VPC), and it isn't the way to segment.

q: A central networking team wants to own and manage a VPC (subnets, route tables, gateways). Application teams in other accounts of the same organization must be able to launch their resources directly into those subnets.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create VPC peering from each application account.
Create a transit gateway and attach a VPC per account.
Use AWS PrivateLink for each application.
Share the subnets with the application accounts by using AWS Resource Access Manager (VPC sharing).
q.k: 'launch resources into another account's subnets' → VPC sharing with RAM
x: Each account would still have its own VPC.
Same: one VPC per account, not a shared one.
Exposes services, but doesn't let you launch resources into another VPC.
With VPC sharing, participant accounts create resources in subnets owned by another account, and the network is managed in one place.

q: A company is designing a secure web tier for an internet-facing application.
Which architecture follows AWS best practices?
o: EC2 instances in public subnets with Elastic IPs and security groups open to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443.
An internet-facing ALB in public subnets in two AZs, EC2 instances in private subnets, and the instances' security group allowing traffic only from the ALB's security group.
An internal ALB in private subnets with instances in public subnets.
A single EC2 instance in a public subnet behind a Route 53 health check.
q.k: public ALB + private instances + chained SGs
x: Exposes every instance directly.
Only the ALB is reachable from the internet, and the instances accept traffic only from the ALB. Multi-AZ.
Backwards: an internal ALB doesn't receive internet traffic.
Single point of failure.
