q: Remote employees must securely access applications that run in private subnets of a VPC from their laptops, authenticating with the corporate identity provider.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: AWS Client VPN with SAML-based federated authentication
q.k: remote individual users → Client VPN
x: Connects networks (office ↔ VPC), not individual laptops.
A dedicated physical link.
Client VPN is a managed OpenVPN-based service with AD, certificate, or SAML authentication.
Would expose the applications to the internet.

q: A team launched an EC2 instance as a NAT instance in a public subnet and pointed the private route tables to it. The route is active, but instances in the private subnets still have no internet access.
What is the MOST likely missing configuration?
o: The NAT instance needs an IAM role.
Source/destination check must be disabled on the NAT instance.
The private subnets need an internet gateway route.
The NAT instance must be in a private subnet.
q.k: NAT instance → disable the source/destination check
x: Not involved in packet forwarding.
By default EC2 drops traffic that doesn't have the instance as source or destination. A NAT forwards other hosts' traffic, so the check must be disabled.
Private subnets must not have a direct route to the IGW.
It must be in a public subnet with a public IP.

q: A data pipeline running in private subnets writes billions of items per month to Amazon DynamoDB in the same Region. All traffic currently goes through a NAT gateway, which generates high data processing charges.
Which change reduces cost the MOST?
o: Create a DynamoDB gateway VPC endpoint and associate it with the private subnets' route tables.
Move the pipeline to public subnets.
Switch DynamoDB to provisioned capacity mode.
q.k: DynamoDB/S3 through NAT → free gateway endpoint
x: Traffic goes straight to DynamoDB through the endpoint, bypassing the NAT, and the gateway endpoint is free.
DAX speeds up reads; it doesn't cut write costs or NAT traffic.
Would save the NAT, but exposes the instances.
Changes capacity cost, not network cost.

q: A small company needs private connectivity to AWS with 300 Mbps of bandwidth within a few weeks, at the lowest cost.
Which option is MOST appropriate?
o: A 10 Gbps dedicated Direct Connect connection
A Direct Connect hosted connection from an AWS Direct Connect Partner
Two Site-to-Site VPN connections with ECMP on a transit gateway
q.k: low-bandwidth DX → hosted connection (partner)
x: Oversized and more expensive.
Partners offer hosted connections at low and mid capacities, and they're usually provisioned faster.
Runs over the internet: not 'private connectivity'.
Not a private link to on-premises.

q: A branch office in Australia uses a Site-to-Site VPN to a transit gateway in eu-west-1. Performance is inconsistent because traffic crosses many internet hops.
Which solution improves VPN performance with the LEAST change?
o: Enable acceleration on the Site-to-Site VPN connection attached to the transit gateway.
Create a CloudFront distribution for the VPN.
Increase the instance size of the customer gateway.
Use VPC peering between the office and eu-west-1.
q.k: distant VPN with poor performance → Accelerated Site-to-Site VPN (TGW only)
x: An accelerated VPN enters the AWS network at the nearest edge location (Global Accelerator). It requires a transit gateway, which already exists.
CloudFront is an HTTP(S) CDN; it doesn't carry IPsec tunnels.
The bottleneck is the internet path.
There's no peering with on-premises networks.

q: A company connects its data center to AWS with one Site-to-Site VPN connection terminating on a single on-premises router. AWS provides two tunnels.
How can the company remove the remaining single point of failure?
o: Add a third tunnel to the same VPN connection.
Do nothing, because the two AWS tunnels already make the solution fully redundant.
Increase the bandwidth of the internet link.
Add a second customer gateway device and create a second VPN connection to it.
q.k: VPN redundancy on the customer side too → second customer gateway
x: Each VPN connection has exactly two tunnels.
The two tunnels protect against failures on the AWS side, not the on-premises router.
Doesn't solve a router failure.
Two devices and two connections remove the single point of failure in your network.

q: A company uses Route 53 failover routing. The primary endpoint is an internal application in a private subnet, which Route 53 health checkers cannot reach.
How can the company health-check the primary endpoint?
o: Open the security group to the Route 53 health checker IP ranges and give the instance a public IP.
Use a Route 53 calculated health check alone.
Create a CloudWatch alarm based on an application or load balancer metric and associate a Route 53 health check with the alarm.
q.k: health check for private resources → health check based on a CloudWatch alarm
x: Exposes a private resource.
A calculated health check combines other health checks; it can't check something unreachable by itself.
Route 53 can evaluate a CloudWatch alarm's state, for example HealthyHostCount of an internal ALB.
Doesn't solve how to check the endpoint.

q: A network ACL has these inbound rules: rule 100 allows TCP 80 from 0.0.0.0/0; rule 200 denies all traffic from 203.0.113.0/24. Traffic from 203.0.113.10 to port 80 still reaches the servers.
How should the NACL be fixed?
o: Change rule 200 to a higher number, such as 300.
Add the deny to the security group instead.
Swap the order of the rules in the console; the order of creation matters.
Renumber the deny rule so that it has a lower number than rule 100, for example 90.
q.k: NACL: evaluated in ascending number order, first match wins
x: The higher the number, the later it's evaluated: allow 100 would still match first.
Security groups don't have deny rules.
What matters is the rule number, not creation order.
With a lower number the deny is evaluated before the allow and that range is blocked.

q: A company created a Route 53 private hosted zone and associated it with a VPC. Instances in the VPC cannot resolve records in the zone.
Which configuration is MOST likely missing?
o: The VPC attributes enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames must be set to true.
The private hosted zone must also be public.
An internet gateway must be attached.
A Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoint must be created.
q.k: private hosted zone doesn't resolve → VPC DNS attributes
x: Private zones require both VPC DNS attributes to be enabled.
Zones are public or private, not both.
Internal DNS resolution doesn't depend on the internet.
Outbound endpoints forward queries out of the VPC; they aren't for resolving your own zones.

q: A company runs an application in one Region and wants to shift slightly more traffic toward a new Region that is geographically farther from some users, without hard percentage splits. Routing should be based on the distance between users and resources, adjustable with a bias value.
Which routing policy meets this requirement?
q.k: distance + 'bias' → geoproximity
x: Weights split by percentage, not distance.
Geoproximity routes by distance, and the bias expands or shrinks the area each resource serves.
Geolocation uses fixed countries or continents, with no bias.
No routing logic.

q: A company wants to prevent EC2 instances in its VPC from accessing S3 buckets that belong to other organizations through the S3 gateway endpoint, to reduce data exfiltration risk.
Which solution meets this requirement with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Add a bucket policy to every bucket in the world.
Remove the S3 gateway endpoint and use a NAT gateway.
Attach an endpoint policy that allows S3 actions only when aws:ResourceOrgID equals the company's organization ID.
Use a security group on the instances that denies S3.
q.k: prevent exfiltration to foreign buckets → endpoint policy with aws:ResourceOrgID
x: You don't control other people's buckets.
With a NAT you lose any control and traffic goes to the internet.
The endpoint policy filters by resource owner. One condition covers all your buckets, current and future.
SGs have no deny and don't filter by bucket.

q: Instances in a VPC are attached to a transit gateway. A solutions architect adds a new VPC attachment, but the new VPC's instances cannot reach other VPCs even though the transit gateway route table already has routes to them.
What is the MOST likely cause?
o: The new VPC's subnet route tables have no route that sends the other VPCs' CIDRs to the transit gateway.
The transit gateway requires VPC peering as well.
q.k: TGW needs routes on both sides (TGW route table and VPC subnet route tables)
x: The real limit is thousands of attachments.
The VPC's subnet route tables must also point to the TGW. A very common miss.
A TGW doesn't need peering.
DNS doesn't affect IP routing.

q: Instances in private subnets in three AZs send about 20 TB per month to an S3 bucket and pull container images from Amazon ECR, all through a single NAT gateway in AZ-a.
Which TWO changes reduce data transfer and NAT costs the MOST? (Select TWO.)
o: Add an S3 gateway endpoint to the private route tables.
Add interface endpoints for ECR (api and dkr) so image pulls avoid the NAT gateway.
Add a NAT gateway in each AZ.
Move the bucket to another Region.
q.k: NAT + S3/ECR traffic → gateway endpoint for S3, interface endpoints for ECR
x: S3 traffic leaves the NAT (no per-GB processing) and the gateway endpoint is free. ECR layers are stored in S3, so this also helps.
ECR API calls go through interface endpoints instead of the NAT; combined with the S3 gateway endpoint, image pulls avoid NAT processing.
Better HA and avoids cross-AZ charges, but adds hourly NAT cost; the endpoints remove most of the traffic instead.
Adds cross-Region transfer cost.
Adds cost and doesn't avoid the NAT.

q: Two application tiers in different AZs exchange several terabytes per day. The network team asks what this costs.
Which statement is correct?
o: Traffic between AZs in the same Region is free.
Data transferred between AZs in the same Region is charged per GB in each direction.
Only traffic over public IPs is charged.
Inter-AZ traffic is charged only when it goes through a NAT gateway.
q.k: cross-AZ transfer is billed (both directions)
x: Only same-AZ traffic over private IPs is free.
Inter-AZ data transfer is billed per GB in and out, which adds up for chatty multi-AZ designs.
Private IP traffic across AZs is still charged.
It's charged regardless of NAT.

q: A company runs a Site-to-Site VPN to a transit gateway with two tunnels. It wants traffic to use both tunnels to get more bandwidth than one tunnel provides.
What should it configure?
o: BGP with equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) enabled on the transit gateway
q.k: aggregate VPN bandwidth → TGW + BGP + ECMP
x: Static routing doesn't spread traffic across tunnels for more bandwidth.
With dynamic routing and ECMP on a transit gateway, traffic is balanced across tunnels and multiple VPN connections.
Unrelated.
Unrelated to VPN.

q: A company uses AWS Direct Connect as its only link to AWS. The link fails for six hours and all hybrid traffic stops.
What is the MOST cost-effective way to keep connectivity during future DX failures?
o: A second Direct Connect connection at the same location
A Site-to-Site VPN as backup over the internet, with routing preferring DX
q.k: cheap DX backup → VPN
x: Same location stays a single point of failure, and costs more.
A VPN costs little and takes over when DX is down (BGP prefers DX when available).
Not reasonable.
Unrelated to hybrid networking.

q: A company's web servers in private subnets must only be reachable through the Application Load Balancer. An auditor finds that the instances' security group allows port 80 from 10.0.0.0/16.
How should the rule be tightened?
o: Allow port 80 only from the ALB's security group.
q.k: only the ALB should reach targets → reference the ALB security group
x: Referencing the ALB's SG allows only traffic coming from the load balancer's nodes.
Opens to everyone.
Breaks the application.
Would also block the ALB, which lives in that range.

q: A company has 50 VPCs attached to a transit gateway. Each VPC deploys its own interface endpoints for 10 AWS services, which costs a lot.
How can the company reduce cost while keeping private access?
o: Centralize the interface endpoints in a shared services VPC, attached to the TGW, and use Route 53 private hosted zones so other VPCs resolve to them.
Delete the endpoints and use public endpoints over a NAT gateway.
Use gateway endpoints for all services.
Peer every VPC with every other VPC.
q.k: many VPCs × many interface endpoints → centralize endpoints in a hub VPC
x: One set of endpoints serves all VPCs through the TGW; private hosted zones point the service names at the central endpoints.
NAT charges per GB and traffic leaves the private path.
Gateway endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB.
Unmanageable and doesn't remove endpoints.

q: Route 53 health checks mark an endpoint unhealthy whenever a single health checker Region has a temporary network issue, causing unneeded failovers.
How can the team make failover decisions more robust?
o: Keep the default behavior where an endpoint is healthy if more than 18% of health checkers report it healthy, and tune the failure threshold and request interval.
q.k: Route 53 health checks aggregate many checkers; tune thresholds instead of disabling
x: Makes failovers more sensitive.
Route 53 uses checkers in many locations and only considers an endpoint unhealthy when most fail; adjusting threshold and interval reduces flapping.
Removes automatic failover.
Removes failover entirely.

q: A company must ensure all traffic leaving its VPCs to the internet is inspected by a central firewall, across 30 VPCs.
Which architecture meets this requirement?
o: An internet gateway in every VPC
A centralized egress (inspection) VPC with AWS Network Firewall and NAT gateways, with all VPCs routing 0.0.0.0/0 through a transit gateway to it
Security groups that deny outbound traffic
q.k: inspect all egress centrally → TGW + inspection/egress VPC
x: Each VPC would bypass central inspection.
A hub inspection VPC with Network Firewall (and NAT) receives all egress through the TGW for consistent policy.
SGs can't inspect or log centrally, and have no deny.
Logs traffic; doesn't inspect or block.

q: A company wants users to reach an application through a single global IP address, even though it runs ALBs in three Regions, with traffic sent to the closest healthy Region.
Which service should be used?
o: AWS Global Accelerator with endpoint groups for each Region's ALB
q.k: static global IPs in front of multi-Region endpoints → Global Accelerator
x: Global Accelerator provides static anycast IPs and routes to the nearest healthy endpoint group over the AWS backbone.
DNS doesn't provide a single static IP.
Regional only.
Unrelated.

q: The company must log all DNS queries made by resources in its VPCs to detect data exfiltration attempts, and block queries to known malicious domains.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Route 53 Resolver query logging plus Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall
q.k: log and filter DNS from VPCs → Resolver query logs + DNS Firewall
x: Query logging records every DNS query; DNS Firewall blocks domains with managed or custom lists.
Flow Logs don't include DNS query names.
SGs don't filter DNS names.
Unrelated.

q: An application on EC2 needs consistent, high network throughput and low latency between instances. The instances run Amazon Linux on a current Nitro instance type.
What must be in place to get enhanced networking?
o: The Elastic Network Adapter (ENA) driver, which current Nitro instances and AMIs support
q.k: higher PPS, lower latency on EC2 → enhanced networking (ENA)
x: Enhanced networking with ENA gives higher bandwidth and lower latency; it's supported on current instance types and AMIs.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.
Unrelated to instance-to-instance throughput.

q: A company deploys a three-tier web application. Which subnet layout provides high availability with the fewest components?
o: One public and one private subnet in a single AZ
Public and private subnets in at least two AZs, with the ALB and Auto Scaling group spanning them
One subnet per tier in one AZ, with backups
Only public subnets in three AZs
q.k: HA starts at two AZs
x: One AZ is a single point of failure.
Spreading the load balancer and instances across two or more AZs survives an AZ failure.
Still one AZ.
Exposes every tier publicly.

q: A company runs a web application on EC2 instances in private subnets across three Availability Zones behind an internet-facing ALB. The instances download patches and call a third-party payment API on the internet. During an outage of one AZ, instances in the healthy AZs could no longer reach the payment API, and orders failed. The company wants to prevent this while keeping costs reasonable.
What should a solutions architect do?
o: Move the instances to public subnets with Elastic IP addresses.
Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each AZ and configure each private subnet's route table to use the NAT gateway in the same AZ.
Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance in an Auto Scaling group of one.
Add a second internet gateway to the VPC.
q.k: egress survives AZ failure → zonal NAT gateways + per-AZ routes
x: Exposes the instances and changes the security posture.
Each AZ has its own NAT, so losing one AZ doesn't affect the others.
Still a single point of failure across AZs, with slow recovery.
A VPC can have only one internet gateway; the IGW wasn't the problem.

q: A healthcare company runs analytics jobs on EC2 instances in private subnets. The jobs read and write large volumes of data in S3 buckets in the same Region. Compliance requires that this traffic never traverses the internet and that the instances can only access the company's own buckets, not arbitrary buckets on S3.
Which combination meets these requirements MOST cost-effectively? (Select TWO.)
o: Create an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and add it to the private subnets' route tables.
Attach an endpoint policy that allows S3 actions only on the company's buckets (or only when aws:ResourceOrgID matches the organization).
Create an S3 interface VPC endpoint in each AZ.
Route S3 traffic through a NAT gateway with a security group.
q.k: private S3 access + restrict which buckets + cheapest → gateway endpoint + endpoint policy
x: Gateway endpoints keep traffic on the AWS network and cost nothing.
The endpoint policy limits access to approved buckets, reducing exfiltration risk.
Works, but has hourly and per-GB charges; the gateway endpoint is cheaper inside the VPC.
Goes through the internet path and can't restrict buckets.
Uses public edge locations.

q: A company has 40 VPCs across 4 Regions and an on-premises data center connected by a single AWS Direct Connect connection in Frankfurt. All VPCs must reach on-premises systems, VPCs in the same Region must reach each other, and the network team wants to manage routing centrally with as few connections as possible.
Which architecture meets these requirements?
o: Full-mesh VPC peering in each Region and a private VIF per VPC.
A transit gateway in each Region with all local VPCs attached, transit gateways peered across Regions, and a Direct Connect gateway associated with the transit gateways through a transit VIF.
A Site-to-Site VPN from on-premises to each VPC.
A single VPC in Frankfurt that routes traffic for all other VPCs.
q.k: many VPCs + many Regions + one DX → TGW per Region + DX gateway (transit VIF) + TGW peering
x: Hundreds of peerings and VIFs, and peering isn't transitive.
Regional TGWs act as hubs, inter-Region peering links them, and one transit VIF via a DX gateway reaches all of them.
Many tunnels to manage, over the internet.
VPC peering isn't transitive, so a transit VPC can't route this way.

q: A company exposes an internal payment service to 300 business customers. Each customer has its own AWS account and VPC, and many use the same CIDR ranges as the company. The service must be reachable privately from customer VPCs, customers must not gain access to any other resource in the company's VPC, and the company wants to approve each customer connection.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: VPC peering with each customer VPC and security groups to restrict access
A transit gateway shared with customers through AWS RAM
An endpoint service (AWS PrivateLink) in front of a Network Load Balancer, with acceptance required, and customers creating interface endpoints
A public ALB restricted with AWS WAF IP sets
q.k: overlapping CIDRs + many consumers + expose one service + approval → PrivateLink endpoint service
x: Overlapping CIDRs make peering impossible, and it would expose the whole VPC.
Would connect networks and fail with overlapping CIDRs.
PrivateLink is one-way, works with overlapping CIDRs, exposes only the service, and supports connection acceptance.
Traffic goes over the internet, not privately.

q: A company serves an API from two Regions. Under normal conditions all traffic must go to us-east-1. If the us-east-1 endpoint becomes unhealthy, traffic must move to eu-west-1 automatically. The API runs behind ALBs, and the company uses Route 53.
Which configuration meets these requirements?
o: Latency-based routing records for both ALBs
Failover routing: a primary alias record for the us-east-1 ALB with Evaluate Target Health (or a health check), and a secondary alias record for the eu-west-1 ALB
Geolocation routing with a default record
q.k: active-passive across Regions → failover routing with health evaluation
x: Sends users to the closest Region, not always to us-east-1.
Primary serves while healthy; Route 53 returns the secondary when the primary fails.
Splits traffic between both Regions.
Routes by user location.

q: After a security incident, a company must ensure that EC2 instances in a set of private subnets can only make outbound HTTPS connections to *.amazonaws.com and to two partner domains. All other outbound traffic must be blocked and logged. The solution must be managed and scale automatically.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Security groups with outbound rules for the partner domains
Network ACLs with the partner IP ranges
AWS Network Firewall in a dedicated firewall subnet with a stateful domain allow-list rule group and logging, and route tables sending egress through the firewall endpoints
A NAT instance running a custom proxy
q.k: egress allow-list by domain + logs + managed → Network Firewall
x: SGs can't filter by domain name.
Partner IPs change, NACLs can't match domains, and logging is limited.
Network Firewall filters TLS SNI/HTTP host against domain lists, logs decisions, and scales as a managed service.
Not managed and a single point of failure.

q: Users in Asia and Europe access a TCP-based trading application hosted in us-east-1. They report high and variable latency. The application doesn't use HTTP, and clients connect to a fixed IP address configured in their firewalls.
Which solution reduces latency with the LEAST change to clients?
o: Amazon CloudFront in front of the application
AWS Global Accelerator with the existing Network Load Balancer as an endpoint, giving clients two static anycast IP addresses
q.k: non-HTTP + global users + static IPs → Global Accelerator
x: CloudFront is for HTTP(S) content.
Users enter the AWS backbone at the nearest edge location and keep fixed IPs.
Needs more Regions to help, and doesn't give static IPs.
For S3 uploads only.

q: A company's on-premises data center connects to AWS through two Direct Connect connections terminating on different devices in the same Direct Connect location. A fire at the colocation facility took both connections down for a day.
What should the company do to avoid a similar outage in the MOST cost-effective way?
o: Add a third connection in the same location.
Add a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup, or move one of the connections to a second Direct Connect location.
Increase the bandwidth of both connections.
Use a LAG for the two existing connections.
q.k: location-level failure → second location (or VPN backup)
x: Same location, same risk.
Location diversity removes the shared failure; a VPN is the cheapest backup path.
Doesn't address location failure.
A LAG stays in one location.

q: An e-commerce company must give its on-call engineers shell access to EC2 instances in private subnets for troubleshooting. Security requires: no inbound ports open, no SSH keys, MFA, and a full record of every command typed.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: A bastion host with SSH key rotation and CloudTrail
AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, with IAM Identity Center (MFA) for access and session logging to CloudWatch Logs or S3
EC2 Instance Connect through public IPs
q.k: no ports, no keys, MFA, command logs → Session Manager
x: Needs inbound SSH and keys; CloudTrail doesn't record typed commands.
Sessions use the SSM agent's outbound connection, IAM controls access, and session data is logged.
Requires public IPs and inbound SSH.
Still SSH keys and open ports in the VPC.

q: A company runs 60 VPCs. Each VPC has its own NAT gateways in three AZs for internet egress, and NAT hourly charges are a large part of the bill. Traffic volumes per VPC are small.
Which change reduces cost the MOST while keeping egress highly available?
o: Remove all NAT gateways and use public subnets.
Centralize egress: attach all VPCs to a transit gateway and route internet traffic to a shared egress VPC with one NAT gateway per AZ.
Use a single NAT gateway in one VPC without a transit gateway.
Replace NAT gateways with interface endpoints.
q.k: many small VPCs paying for NAT → centralized egress VPC
x: Exposes workloads.
Replaces 180 NAT gateways with 3, keeping per-AZ HA; TGW data processing is small for low volumes.
Other VPCs can't route to it without a TGW, and it isn't HA.
Interface endpoints reach AWS services, not the internet.

q: A company runs a tightly coupled high performance computing (HPC) simulation on 32 EC2 instances. The nodes exchange large amounts of data and require the lowest possible network latency and highest throughput between them.
Which configuration meets these requirements?
o: Launch the instances in a spread placement group across three Availability Zones.
Launch the instances in a cluster placement group in a single Availability Zone, using instances that support Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA).
Launch the instances in a partition placement group with one instance per partition.
Launch the instances in an Auto Scaling group across all Availability Zones in the Region.
q.k: tightly coupled HPC, lowest latency → cluster placement group (+ EFA)
x: Spread places instances on distinct hardware, often across AZs: maximum isolation, not minimum latency.
Cluster placement groups pack instances close together in one AZ for low-latency, high-bandwidth networking. EFA adds OS-bypass for MPI workloads.
Partition groups isolate groups of instances for large distributed systems such as HDFS or Cassandra; not built for lowest latency.
Spreading across AZs increases latency between nodes.

q: A company runs a small number of critical EC2 instances that must not fail at the same time because of a single hardware failure. There are fewer than seven instances per Availability Zone.
Which placement strategy should be used?
o: No placement group, with Dedicated Hosts
q.k: few critical instances, no shared hardware → spread placement group (max 7 per AZ)
x: Packs instances together: one rack failure can take several down.
Groups instances in partitions; instances in the same partition share hardware. Built for large distributed systems.
Each instance is placed on distinct hardware (separate racks), up to 7 running instances per AZ per group.
Dedicated Hosts are about licensing and isolation from other customers, not about spreading across racks.

q: A company runs a large Apache Cassandra cluster of 90 nodes on EC2. It wants to reduce the chance that a rack-level hardware failure affects replicas of the same data, and it needs to know which instances share racks.
Which placement strategy meets these requirements?
o: Partition placement group, mapping Cassandra racks to partitions
Launch all nodes as Dedicated Instances
q.k: large distributed, topology-aware (HDFS, HBase, Cassandra) → partition placement group
x: Partitions don't share racks with each other, and EC2 exposes the partition number so the database can place replicas in different partitions.
Increases the blast radius of a rack failure.
Limited to 7 instances per AZ per group: too small for 90 nodes, and no partition topology.
Dedicated Instances don't give rack-level placement control.

q: A company runs a nightly batch job that processes image files. The job can be interrupted and restarted without data loss, and it can run on any of several instance types. The company wants the lowest compute cost.
Which purchasing option should be used?
o: Spot Instances with a diversified allocation across several instance types
q.k: interruptible + flexible + cheapest → Spot (diversified)
x: Works, but costs much more than Spot.
Commits to 24/7 capacity for a job that runs a few hours a night.
The most expensive option, used for licensing or compliance.
Spot offers the deepest discounts for fault-tolerant work. Diversifying instance types reduces interruptions.

q: A company's EC2 usage is steady at about 40 instances, but the team regularly changes instance families and moves some workloads to AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. Finance wants a 1-year commitment with the largest discount that still allows this flexibility.
Which option should the company buy?
o: Standard Reserved Instances for the current instance types
q.k: commitment + flexibility across families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda → Compute Savings Plans
x: Standard RIs are tied to an instance family (and Region); they don't cover Fargate or Lambda.
Compute Savings Plans apply to any instance family, size, OS, Region, and also to Fargate and Lambda.
Bigger discount, but locked to one instance family in one Region and no Fargate or Lambda.
Not a commitment and can be interrupted.

q: A company must be sure it can launch 20 instances of a specific type in a specific Availability Zone during a two-week product launch. It does not want a long-term commitment.
Which option meets these requirements?
o: Buy 1-year Reserved Instances scoped to the Region.
Request Spot Instances with a maximum price.
Create an On-Demand Capacity Reservation for the two weeks.
q.k: guaranteed capacity in an AZ, short term, no commitment → On-Demand Capacity Reservation
x: Regional RIs give a discount but don't reserve capacity, and need a 1-year term.
Spot never guarantees capacity.
Capacity Reservations hold capacity in a specific AZ for as long as you need, with no term commitment. You pay On-Demand rates while active.
A Savings Plan is a billing discount, not reserved capacity.

q: A company wants to bring its existing per-socket and per-core Windows Server and SQL Server licenses to AWS. It needs visibility into the physical sockets and cores of the servers it runs on.
Which option meets these requirements?
q.k: BYOL per socket or core → Dedicated Hosts
x: They run on hardware dedicated to you, but don't expose sockets and cores or give control over placement.
Dedicated Hosts give a physical server with visibility of sockets and cores, which per-socket or per-core licensing needs.
Shared hardware and interruptible.
Shared hardware; no visibility into sockets or cores.

q: An Auto Scaling group runs a web application. The team wants the group to keep average CPU utilization at 50% automatically, adding and removing instances as needed, with the least configuration.
Which scaling policy should be used?
o: Simple scaling with a CloudWatch alarm at 80% CPU
Target tracking scaling with a target of 50% average CPU
q.k: 'keep metric at X' → target tracking
x: Reacts to one threshold and waits for cooldowns; it doesn't keep a target.
Ignores the actual load.
Works, but you must define the alarms and steps yourself.
Target tracking creates and manages the alarms and adjusts capacity to keep the metric near the target, like a thermostat.

q: Traffic to an application rises sharply every weekday at 08:00 and falls at 18:00. New instances take 5 minutes to become ready, so users see slow responses each morning while the Auto Scaling group catches up.
Which solution fixes this with the LEAST operational effort?
o: Add scheduled actions (or predictive scaling) that raise capacity before 08:00 and lower it after 18:00.
Lower the CPU threshold of the existing simple scaling policy to 20%.
Replace the Auto Scaling group with a single large instance.
q.k: known recurring pattern + slow warm-up → scheduled or predictive scaling
x: Capacity is ready before the spike arrives. Predictive scaling learns the daily pattern and does this automatically.
Scales out earlier, but still reacts after load arrives, and wastes money all day.
Doesn't remove the warm-up delay when traffic rises.
Single point of failure and no elasticity.

q: An application's instances take 10 minutes to boot and load a large cache. Scale-out events are therefore slow. The company wants faster scale-out without paying for fully running idle instances.
Which feature should be used?
o: An Auto Scaling warm pool with instances kept in the Stopped (or Hibernated) state
q.k: slow initialization + fast scale-out + low cost → warm pool
x: Slows scaling down further.
Only helps for predictable times.
A warm pool keeps pre-initialized instances ready. Stopped instances cost only their EBS storage and start much faster than new ones.
Placement has nothing to do with boot time.

q: Instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer sometimes hang: the OS is running, but the application returns errors. The Auto Scaling group keeps these instances because EC2 status checks pass.
How can the company automatically replace these instances?
o: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances.
Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group.
Add a lifecycle hook for instance launch.
q.k: unhealthy app but EC2 checks pass → use ELB health checks in the ASG
x: More frequent metrics; doesn't change health decisions.
With ELB health checks enabled, the ASG also treats an instance as unhealthy when the load balancer's health check fails, and replaces it.
Doesn't fix the hang detection.
Lifecycle hooks pause launches or terminations for custom actions; they don't detect application failure.

q: Before an instance in an Auto Scaling group is terminated during scale-in, the application must upload its local log files to Amazon S3.
Which feature should be used?
o: A termination lifecycle hook that pauses termination while a script uploads the logs
Instance scale-in protection on all instances
q.k: run custom action before launch or termination → lifecycle hook
x: The hook puts the instance in Terminating:Wait until the action completes (or a timeout), then termination continues.
User data runs at launch, not at termination.
Changes capacity at set times; it doesn't run actions on instances.
Prevents scale-in entirely.

q: A company hosts several microservices behind one load balancer. Requests to /api/orders/* must go to the orders service and /api/users/* to the users service. Requests to admin.example.com must go to an admin service.
Which load balancer meets these requirements?
o: Network Load Balancer with listeners per port
Application Load Balancer with path-based and host-based listener rules
q.k: path or host routing (layer 7) → ALB
x: Layer 4: it doesn't see HTTP paths or hostnames.
For inserting virtual appliances, not for HTTP routing.
Legacy, no listener rules for content routing.
ALB rules route by path, host header, HTTP headers, query strings, and more, to different target groups.

q: A multiplayer game server uses a custom UDP protocol and needs to handle millions of requests per second with ultra-low latency. Clients' firewalls allow only fixed IP addresses.
Which load balancer should be used?
o: Network Load Balancer with an Elastic IP address per Availability Zone
q.k: UDP/TCP, extreme performance, static IPs → NLB
x: NLB works at layer 4 (TCP, UDP, TLS), handles millions of requests per second, and supports one static or Elastic IP per AZ.
ALB is HTTP/HTTPS only and has no static IPs.
Legacy and no UDP.
A CDN for HTTP(S) content.

q: A legacy web application stores user session data in memory on each EC2 instance. Users behind an Application Load Balancer are logged out when their requests reach a different instance. The company cannot change the application now.
What is the quickest fix?
o: Enable sticky sessions (session affinity) on the target group.
Switch to a Network Load Balancer.
q.k: in-memory sessions, can't change code → sticky sessions (long-term: externalize to ElastiCache/DynamoDB)
x: Distributes traffic evenly across AZs; doesn't keep a user on one instance.
Stickiness uses a cookie to route a user to the same target. Quick fix; the better long-term design stores sessions in ElastiCache or DynamoDB.
Doesn't solve session affinity.
Lets in-flight requests finish when a target is deregistered; unrelated.

q: During deployments, instances are removed from an Application Load Balancer target group while they are still serving long-running requests, and users see errors.
Which setting should be adjusted?
o: Deregistration delay (connection draining) on the target group
q.k: in-flight requests cut on deregistration → deregistration delay
x: Controls how often health is checked.
Controls how long a user sticks to a target.
The ALB stops sending new requests to the deregistering target and waits up to this delay for in-flight requests to complete.
Controls how long idle connections stay open.

q: An internet-facing Application Load Balancer must serve HTTPS for several domains (shop.example.com, blog.example.org) with separate certificates, all on port 443.
How should this be configured?
o: Use a Network Load Balancer with TCP passthrough only.
Add multiple certificates from AWS Certificate Manager to the HTTPS listener; the ALB selects the certificate with SNI.
Install the certificates on every EC2 instance and use HTTP on the listener.
q.k: several TLS domains on one listener → multiple certificates + SNI
x: Works, but costs more and isn't needed.
Pushes TLS to the instances and loses layer 7 features.
An ALB HTTPS listener supports multiple certificates and uses Server Name Indication to pick the right one.
Traffic from client to ALB would be unencrypted.

q: A Lambda function processes uploaded videos. Some videos take about 40 minutes to process, and the function times out.
What should a solutions architect recommend?
o: Increase the Lambda timeout to 60 minutes.
Increase the function's memory to the maximum.
Run the processing in containers on AWS Fargate (for example, ECS tasks or AWS Batch) triggered by the upload event.
q.k: Lambda max 15 minutes → longer jobs go to Fargate/ECS/Batch
x: The maximum Lambda timeout is 15 minutes.
More memory (and CPU) can speed it up, but a 40-minute job won't fit in 15 minutes reliably.
Removes cold starts; it doesn't extend the timeout.
Fargate tasks have no 15-minute limit and run serverless containers. An event can start them directly.

q: A latency-sensitive API runs on AWS Lambda. Traffic is predictable during business hours, but the first requests after idle periods are slow because of cold starts.
Which solution reduces this latency?
o: Configure provisioned concurrency for the function, scheduled for business hours with Application Auto Scaling.
Move the function into a VPC.
q.k: cold starts on a latency-sensitive function → provisioned concurrency
x: Provisioned concurrency keeps execution environments initialized. Scheduling it for business hours controls cost.
The timeout doesn't affect startup.
Reserved concurrency caps the function; with 1 it would throttle.
Doesn't help cold starts.

q: A Lambda function writes to a relational database that supports at most 50 concurrent connections. During traffic spikes, the function scales out and exhausts the database connections.
Which TWO actions together protect the database? (Select TWO.)
o: Set reserved concurrency on the function to limit its maximum concurrent executions.
Put Amazon RDS Proxy between the function and the database.
Move the function out of the VPC.
q.k: Lambda overwhelming a DB → cap concurrency + RDS Proxy pooling
x: Reserved concurrency sets an upper bound on concurrent executions, which caps connection demand.
RDS Proxy pools and shares database connections across many invocations.
Doesn't change the number of connections.
Makes the problem worse.
Network location doesn't change connection counts.

q: A company wants to run containerized microservices without managing servers, clusters of EC2 instances, or patching.
Which option meets these requirements?
o: Amazon EKS with self-managed node groups
Amazon ECS (or EKS) with the AWS Fargate launch type
Docker installed on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group
q.k: containers without managing servers → Fargate
x: You manage and patch the EC2 container instances.
You manage the nodes.
Fargate runs each task or pod on AWS-managed compute: no instances to provision, scale, or patch.
Fully self-managed.

q: A company already runs Kubernetes on premises with Helm charts and Kubernetes tooling. It wants to move to AWS with minimal changes to its deployment process.
Which service should it use?
q.k: existing Kubernetes tooling → EKS
x: ECS uses its own API and task definitions; it would require rewriting deployments.
A PaaS for web apps; it doesn't run Kubernetes manifests.
Runs web services from source or images, not Kubernetes workloads.
EKS is managed, upstream-conformant Kubernetes, so Helm and kubectl keep working.

q: Researchers submit thousands of independent compute jobs with varying CPU and memory needs. The company wants a managed service that queues the jobs, provisions the right compute (including Spot), and scales it to zero when idle.
Which service meets these requirements?
o: An Auto Scaling group with a scheduled action
q.k: many batch jobs + queue + managed provisioning → AWS Batch
x: Batch manages job queues, scheduling, and compute environments (EC2, Spot, or Fargate) and scales down when idle.
Orchestrates workflows; it doesn't provision compute for a queue of jobs.
For big data frameworks (Spark, Hadoop).
No job queue or scheduling.

q: A small team wants to deploy a Java web application quickly. AWS should handle capacity provisioning, load balancing, scaling, and health monitoring, while the team keeps the option to access the underlying EC2 instances.
Which service meets these requirements?
q.k: upload code, AWS handles infra, still access EC2 → Elastic Beanstalk
x: No access to underlying servers, and a traditional Java web app would need rework.
Beanstalk provisions the ALB, ASG, and monitoring for you, and the resources stay visible and accessible in your account.
Everything is manual.
Infrastructure as code, but you must design the whole stack.

q: An application on a memory-heavy EC2 instance takes 15 minutes to load data into memory after each start. The instance is stopped every night to save costs.
How can startup time be reduced while still stopping the instance at night?
o: Use EC2 hibernation so the RAM contents are saved to the encrypted EBS root volume.
q.k: preserve in-memory state across stop/start → hibernation
x: Hibernation writes RAM to the EBS root volume and restores it on start, so processes resume where they left off. The root volume must be encrypted and large enough.
An AMI doesn't capture RAM.
Instance store data is lost when stopping.
Loading would still take time.

q: A company wants to run the same application in a DR Region. It uses a custom AMI in eu-west-1.
What must it do to launch the AMI in eu-central-1?
o: Share the AMI with the other Region using AWS RAM.
Take a new EBS snapshot in eu-central-1.
q.k: AMIs are regional → copy the AMI
x: AMIs are Regional resources.
RAM doesn't move AMIs between Regions.
There's nothing in eu-central-1 to snapshot.
Copying the AMI (and its snapshots) makes it available in the target Region. Can be automated, for example with Data Lifecycle Manager.

q: A company wants recommendations for right-sizing its EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, EBS volumes, and Lambda functions based on actual utilization.
Which service provides this?
q.k: right-sizing recommendations from utilization → Compute Optimizer
x: Cost Explorer shows spend and some RI and Savings Plan recommendations, but Compute Optimizer is the right-sizing service.
Compute Optimizer analyzes CloudWatch metrics and recommends instance types, sizes, and settings.
Alerts on spend thresholds.
Security vulnerabilities.

q: A company runs Linux-based microservices on x86 EC2 instances. The code is interpreted (Python and Node.js), and the company wants better price-performance with minimal changes.
What should a solutions architect recommend?
q.k: better price-performance, portable code → Graviton
x: More expensive.
Graviton instances typically offer better price-performance, and interpreted languages usually run without code changes.
GPUs are for ML and graphics, and cost more.
More cost, not better price-performance.

q: An application needs extremely high random I/O performance on a temporary scratch dataset that can be regenerated if lost.
Which storage option gives the highest I/O performance at the lowest cost?
q.k: temporary, regenerable, max IOPS → instance store
x: Good general purpose, but network-attached and lower performance than local NVMe.
Very high performance, but expensive for a scratch dataset that doesn't need durability.
Shared network file system; not the fastest.
Instance store is physically attached, delivers very high IOPS, and is included in the instance price. Data is lost when the instance stops or fails, which is acceptable here.

q: A video streaming company must serve users in a large city with single-digit millisecond latency for parts of its application, while keeping the rest of the application in the parent Region.
Which option meets this requirement?
o: Deploy the latency-sensitive components in an AWS Local Zone near the city.
Use a larger instance type in the Region.
Use AWS Outposts in the company's data center.
q.k: single-digit ms latency to end users in a metro → Local Zones
x: Local Zones extend a Region to metro areas, close to end users, and connect to the parent Region.
Doesn't reduce distance to users.
Outposts brings AWS into your own data center, for on-premises needs, not to be near end users in a city.
Affects latency between instances, not to users.

q: A manufacturer must process data on premises because of data residency rules and needs low-latency access to local systems, but wants to use the same AWS APIs, tools, and services it uses in the Region.
Which option meets these requirements?
q.k: AWS infrastructure in your own data center → Outposts
x: Local Zones are AWS-operated metro locations, not your data center.
Wavelength embeds compute in 5G telco networks.
Outposts racks or servers run AWS services on premises with the same APIs and console.
Snowball is for data transfer and edge computing in disconnected locations, not a full on-premises AWS extension.

q: An Auto Scaling group spans three Availability Zones with 6 instances. One AZ becomes unavailable.
What does the Auto Scaling group do?
o: It launches replacement instances in the remaining healthy AZs to maintain the desired capacity.
It terminates all instances and starts again.
It moves the existing instances to another AZ.
q.k: ASG across AZs self-heals by launching in healthy AZs
x: Auto Scaling acts on its own.
Auto Scaling replaces unhealthy instances and keeps desired capacity in the AZs that are available. When the AZ recovers, it rebalances.
It doesn't restart the whole group.
Instances can't be moved between AZs.

q: An event-driven function must run whenever an object is uploaded to S3, resize the image, and write the result to another bucket. Uploads are spiky and unpredictable.
Which compute option is MOST suitable with the LEAST operational overhead?
o: An EC2 instance polling S3 every minute
AWS Lambda triggered by S3 event notifications
An Auto Scaling group with scheduled scaling
q.k: short, event-driven, spiky → Lambda
x: Polling, idle cost, and servers to manage.
Runs and costs even when idle.
Lambda is invoked per event, scales automatically with uploads, and costs nothing when idle.
Doesn't follow unpredictable spikes.

q: A company runs a stateless web application on EC2 behind an ALB. After a marketing email, traffic jumps tenfold within two minutes and the target tracking policy cannot add capacity quickly enough.
Which change helps the MOST?
o: Increase the health check grace period.
Use a launch template with a pre-baked AMI so new instances boot fast, and combine target tracking with a warm pool or a higher minimum during campaigns.
q.k: slow scale-out under sudden spikes → shorter boot (golden AMI), warm pools, pre-scale
x: Delays health replacement; doesn't add capacity.
Faster boot plus pre-warmed or pre-scaled capacity lets the group absorb sudden spikes.
Unrelated to capacity.
Slows scaling.

q: A company runs a web tier with a stable baseline of 10 instances 24/7 and short daily peaks of up to 30 instances. It wants to minimize cost.
Which purchasing mix is MOST cost-effective?
o: A Savings Plan or Reserved Instances for the 10-instance baseline, and On-Demand or Spot for the peaks
q.k: steady baseline → commitment; variable peaks → On-Demand/Spot
x: Pays full price for the predictable baseline.
Pays for 20 instances that sit idle most of the day.
Commit for what runs always and use flexible capacity for the rest. Spot is good for peaks if the app tolerates interruptions.
The baseline could be interrupted, which is risky for a web tier.

q: A web application in an Auto Scaling group needs a mix of On-Demand and Spot Instances across several instance types, with at least 4 On-Demand instances always running.
How should the group be configured?
o: Create two separate Auto Scaling groups and split traffic with Route 53.
Use a mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base capacity of 4, an On-Demand/Spot percentage above the base, and multiple instance types.
Use a launch configuration with Spot pricing.
q.k: On-Demand + Spot + several types in one ASG → mixed instances policy
x: Unnecessary complexity.
A mixed instances policy sets the On-Demand base, the split above it, the Spot allocation strategy, and multiple instance types in one group.
Doesn't guarantee the On-Demand base the way the ASG policy does, and loses ASG features.
Launch configurations are legacy and don't support mixed instances.

q: A Spot-based processing fleet must gracefully finish or checkpoint work when an instance is about to be reclaimed.
What should the application do?
o: Monitor for the two-minute Spot Instance interruption notice (instance metadata or EventBridge) and checkpoint work when it arrives.
Request Spot Instances with a higher maximum price so they're never reclaimed.
q.k: Spot interruption → 2-minute notice, checkpoint
x: AWS sends a 2-minute warning through instance metadata and an EventBridge event, which the app can use to checkpoint or drain.
Spot can still be reclaimed for capacity; price doesn't guarantee anything.
Instance store data is lost with the instance.
Irrelevant.

q: A company wants to deploy a containerized web API from a container image with automatic HTTPS, load balancing, and scaling, without configuring clusters, load balancers, or networking.
Which service has the LEAST operational overhead?
q.k: container image → running HTTPS service, zero infra config → App Runner
x: Still requires a cluster, ingress, and networking configuration.
You manage EC2 instances and the load balancer.
App Runner builds and runs web services from source or an image and handles TLS, load balancing, and scaling for you.
Fully manual.

q: A company deploys a new version of an application in an Auto Scaling group and wants to replace instances gradually while keeping at least 90% of capacity healthy, with automatic rollback if health checks fail.
Which feature should be used?
o: Instance refresh with a minimum healthy percentage and auto rollback

q: An application must call a Lambda function synchronously from an HTTPS client with a simple dedicated HTTPS endpoint, without API keys, throttling rules, or request transformation.

o: Amazon API Gateway REST API with a Lambda integration
An Application Load Balancer with a Lambda target
Amazon CloudFront with an S3 origin

A function URL is a built-in HTTPS endpoint for a single function, with IAM or no auth.

q: A development team runs 30 EC2 instances that are only used from 08:00 to 19:00 on weekdays.

Stopped instances don't incur compute charges (EBS still billed), cutting most of the cost.
More expensive.

q: A stateless web tier on an Auto Scaling group runs 6 On-Demand instances at baseline and scales to 30 during peaks. The application handles interruptions gracefully.
Which configuration is MOST cost-effective?

All Spot with one instance type

x: Pays full price for everything.
Commitment covers the always-on base; Spot covers bursts cheaply; diversification and capacity-optimized allocation reduce interruptions.
A single type increases interruption risk, and the base could be interrupted.
Pays for capacity idle most of the time.

q: A Lambda function runs millions of times per day and is CPU-bound. The team wants to reduce cost without changing the code.

o: Switch the function to the arm64 (Graviton) architecture and tune memory with a power-tuning test.
Move it to a larger EC2 instance.
q.k: Lambda cost → arm64 + right-size memory
x: Doesn't change cost per invocation.
arm64 is priced lower per GB-second and often faster; tuning memory finds the cheapest configuration since CPU scales with memory.
Adds a fixed cost.
Adds servers to manage.

q: An application on a single EC2 instance must recover automatically if the underlying hardware fails, keeping the same private IP, instance ID, and EBS volumes. It cannot be placed behind a load balancer.

q.k: single instance, same identity after hardware failure → EC2 auto recovery

Restores old data and requires manual work.
Can be interrupted.
Instance store data is lost on hardware failure.

q: An Auto Scaling group runs in a single AZ to keep latency low between nodes. Management now requires the application to survive an AZ failure.

With subnets in several AZs, the group spreads instances and replaces capacity in healthy AZs.
Doesn't add resilience.
Keeps everything in one AZ.

q: An application's response time degrades when CPU exceeds 70%, but its Auto Scaling group scales on CPU above 90%. Scaling actions happen too late.

Slows scaling further.
Doesn't affect when scaling happens.
Unrelated.

q: A video transcoding service uses EC2 GPU instances only when jobs arrive, sometimes once a week. Jobs take 2 hours and must not be lost if capacity is interrupted.
Which solution is MOST cost-effective and reliable?
o: Use AWS Batch with a compute environment that scales to zero, using Spot with retries and an On-Demand fallback queue.
q.k: rare, long batch jobs → Batch scaling to zero (+ Spot with retries)
x: Pays for idle GPUs most of the week.
Batch launches GPUs only when jobs are queued, uses cheaper Spot, retries interrupted jobs, and can fall back to On-Demand.
15-minute limit and no GPU.
Expensive and still idle.

q: An ALB distributes traffic across two AZs. AZ-a has 2 targets and AZ-b has 8 targets, and AZ-a's targets are overloaded.

That the ALB has an Elastic IP
q.k: uneven targets per AZ → cross-zone load balancing
x: With cross-zone on, every node spreads across all targets evenly; if it was turned off, each AZ's targets get half the traffic.
Stickiness doesn't balance targets.
ALBs don't use EIPs.
Unrelated.

q: A Lambda function processes SQS messages. Some messages always fail and are retried forever, blocking the processing of others in the same batch.

o: Configure a dead-letter queue on the SQS queue with a maxReceiveCount.
Enable ReportBatchItemFailures in the event source mapping so only failed messages are retried.

x: Messages that fail repeatedly move to the DLQ.
Partial batch responses stop successful messages from being reprocessed with the failed ones.
Doesn't fix failing messages.
Stops all processing.
FIFO would make a failing message block its group even more.

q: A Java Lambda function has cold starts of several seconds because of framework initialization. The team wants to reduce startup latency without paying for always-on environments.

x: SnapStart snapshots an initialized environment and resumes from it, cutting cold start time.
Caps concurrency; doesn't speed startup.

Unrelated.

q: A company runs ECS tasks on Fargate 24/7 with predictable usage, and also runs fault-tolerant batch tasks.
Which TWO options reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
o: Buy a Compute Savings Plan covering the steady Fargate usage.
Run the fault-tolerant batch tasks on Fargate Spot.
q.k: Fargate discounts → Compute Savings Plans + Fargate Spot
x: Compute Savings Plans apply to Fargate.
Fargate Spot is much cheaper for interruptible tasks.
RIs don't apply to Fargate.
Not applicable to Fargate.
Increases cost.

q: A stateful legacy application runs on one EC2 instance and can't scale horizontally. The company wants automatic replacement if the instance becomes unhealthy, with minimal cost.

o: An Auto Scaling group with min = max = desired = 1, using a launch template and data on EFS or an EBS restore process
q.k: self-healing single instance → ASG of 1

The app can't run two copies.
Doesn't self-heal.
Slow and manual.

q: A media company runs a video rendering farm on EC2. Jobs arrive in unpredictable bursts, take 20–40 minutes each, can be restarted from a checkpoint, and must finish within 6 hours of submission. The company wants to minimize cost and operational overhead.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: An Auto Scaling group of On-Demand instances with scheduled scaling
AWS Batch with a managed compute environment using Spot Instances across several instance types, with a job retry strategy, and a second On-Demand compute environment as fallback
Lambda functions orchestrated by Step Functions
A fixed fleet of Reserved Instances sized for the peak
q.k: bursty, restartable batch, cost first → Batch + diversified Spot + retries
x: Pays On-Demand prices and can't predict bursts.
Batch queues jobs and scales to zero; diversified Spot is cheapest, retries cover interruptions, and On-Demand fallback protects the deadline.
Exceeds Lambda's 15-minute limit.
Pays for peak capacity that sits idle.

q: A company runs a stateless web application on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB across two AZs. Users report errors during deployments. Investigation shows that new instances receive traffic before the application has finished loading its cache, which takes 3 minutes after boot.
Which TWO changes fix this? (Select TWO.)
o: Configure a health check grace period (or a launch lifecycle hook) so instances aren't considered in service until they're ready.
Configure the ALB target group health check to call an endpoint that returns success only after the cache is loaded.
q.k: traffic before app is ready → readiness health check + grace period/lifecycle hook
x: Gives the instance time to warm up before Auto Scaling evaluates health or adds it to service.
The ALB sends traffic only to targets that pass a real readiness check.
Loads the cache faster at best.
Unrelated.
Doesn't stop traffic to unready instances.

q: A company runs three workloads on EC2: a production web tier that runs 24/7 at a steady 20 instances of m6i.large, a nightly batch job that can tolerate interruptions, and a new service whose instance family will change over the next year as the team experiments with Graviton and containers on Fargate.
Which purchasing strategy minimizes cost while fitting each workload?
o: EC2 Instance Savings Plan for the web tier, Spot Instances for the batch job, and a Compute Savings Plan for the new service
Standard Reserved Instances for all three workloads
q.k: steady fixed family → EC2 Instance SP; interruptible → Spot; changing family/Fargate → Compute SP
x: Most expensive.
Each workload gets the cheapest option that matches its flexibility needs.
RIs lock family and don't cover Fargate; batch would overpay.
The web tier can't tolerate interruptions.

q: An image-processing API runs on Lambda behind API Gateway. At peak, it receives 3,000 requests per second, each taking 2 seconds. Users report throttling errors (429) during peaks, while the account's other functions also slow down.

Move the function into a VPC.
q.k: concurrency = rate × duration (3,000 × 2 = 6,000) > default quota → raise quota + reserved concurrency
x: Doesn't add concurrency.
Required concurrency exceeds the default regional limit (1,000); reserving concurrency protects other functions.
Unrelated.
Images processed per request are usually unique; caching won't help.

q: A gaming company needs to host session servers for a real-time multiplayer game over UDP. Players connect directly to a server by IP. The servers must scale with demand, and the company wants the fewest moving parts.
Which solution fits BEST?
o: An Application Load Balancer in front of an Auto Scaling group
A Network Load Balancer with UDP listeners in front of an Auto Scaling group
q.k: UDP traffic → NLB
x: ALB only handles HTTP/HTTPS.
NLB supports UDP at layer 4 with static IPs per AZ and integrates with Auto Scaling.
WebSocket over HTTP, not raw UDP.
CloudFront isn't for UDP game traffic.

q: A company runs a legacy application on a single large EC2 instance that writes state to its local instance store. The instance was stopped for maintenance, and all state was lost. The application can't be redesigned this quarter.
What should a solutions architect recommend to prevent data loss with minimal changes?

q.k: data lost on stop → instance store is ephemeral → use EBS
x: EBS persists independently of the instance lifecycle; snapshots protect against volume loss.
Hibernation needs an EBS root and doesn't save instance store data.
Makes interruptions more likely.
Restores week-old data.

q: A company runs microservices on Amazon ECS with the EC2 launch type. Cluster instances are often underused, and the team spends time patching AMIs and right-sizing the cluster. Workloads are steady and don't need GPUs or special kernels.

o: Move the services to the Fargate launch type.
Move to EKS with self-managed nodes.
q.k: stop managing container hosts → Fargate
x: Fargate removes cluster instances, patching and bin-packing; you pay per task.
Still managing nodes, plus Kubernetes.
More waste.
More cost and management.

q: An application on EC2 behind an ALB is deployed by replacing instances. The company wants zero-downtime releases with the ability to switch back to the previous version within seconds if errors increase.
Which approach meets these requirements?
o: Blue/green: run the new version in a second target group (or Auto Scaling group) and shift ALB listener weights between target groups, rolling back by shifting weights back
Terminate all instances and launch new ones
Deploy in place on each instance with SSH
q.k: instant rollback → blue/green with weighted target groups
x: Both versions stay running; weighted target groups move traffic gradually and back instantly.
Causes downtime.
Slow and risky rollback.
Unrelated to deployments.

q: A company needs to run a Windows .NET Framework web application that requires IIS and a domain join. It wants AWS to handle provisioning, load balancing and auto scaling, with the least operational overhead.

Amazon ECS on Fargate with Linux containers
q.k: managed platform for Windows/IIS apps → Elastic Beanstalk (Windows)
x: Not for IIS-hosted .NET Framework apps.
Beanstalk supports .NET on Windows/IIS and manages the ALB and ASG.
Linux containers and source runtimes only.
.NET Framework needs Windows.

q: A company runs a CPU-intensive workload on c5.4xlarge instances at 15% average CPU. Memory use is also low. The workload is a Java service that runs on Linux.

Test a Graviton-based instance family (for example c7g) for better price-performance.
Increase the instance size to reduce scaling events.
Switch to an io2 root volume.
q.k: low utilization + portable runtime → right-size + Graviton
x: Compute Optimizer suggests smaller, cheaper instance types based on usage.
Java runs on Arm, and Graviton usually costs less for the same performance.
More expensive.
More waste.
More expensive storage.

q: A company stores application logs in Amazon S3. Logs are queried often for 30 days, rarely between 30 and 90 days, and must be kept for 7 years for compliance, with retrieval within 12 hours acceptable after 90 days.
Which lifecycle configuration is MOST cost-effective?
o: Keep everything in S3 Standard for 7 years.
S3 Standard, then S3 Standard-IA after 30 days, then S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 90 days, and expire after 7 years.
S3 One Zone-IA from day one, then delete after 90 days.
q.k: known access pattern + long archive with hours to retrieve → Standard → IA → Deep Archive
x: Most expensive option for data that is almost never read.
Matches each phase: frequent access, infrequent access, then the cheapest archive (Deep Archive retrieval within 12 hours standard, 48 hours bulk), and expiration at the end of retention.
Deleting after 90 days breaks the 7-year retention requirement.
Good for unknown patterns; here the pattern is known, and lifecycle to Deep Archive is cheaper for long archives.

q: A data lake in S3 has thousands of objects with unpredictable, changing access patterns. Some objects are read heavily for a while, then not at all. The company wants to optimize storage cost automatically without retrieval fees or operational effort.
Which storage class should be used?
q.k: unknown or changing access patterns → Intelligent-Tiering
x: Has retrieval fees, and it's wrong for frequently accessed objects.
Archive class: retrieval takes minutes to hours.
Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically based on use, with no retrieval fees (small monitoring fee per object).
Single-AZ, retrieval fees, and still a fixed tier.

q: A company stores medical images that are rarely accessed, but when a doctor needs one, it must be available within milliseconds.
Which storage class is MOST cost-effective?
q.k: rarely accessed + millisecond retrieval → Glacier Instant Retrieval
x: Archive pricing with millisecond access, designed for data accessed about once a quarter.
Retrieval takes hours.
Millisecond access, but more expensive for rarely accessed data.
Retrieval takes minutes to hours.

q: A company keeps secondary copies of thumbnails that can be regenerated from the originals. They are accessed infrequently, and the company wants the lowest cost for millisecond access.
Which storage class should be used?
q.k: re-creatable + infrequent → One Zone-IA
x: Pays for frequent-access pricing.
Multi-AZ resilience the data doesn't need.
Stored in one AZ, cheaper than Standard-IA. Acceptable because the data can be regenerated if the AZ is lost.
Retrieval takes hours.

q: Regulations require that financial records in S3 cannot be deleted or overwritten by anyone, including the root user, for 5 years.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Use a bucket policy that denies s3:DeleteObject.
Enable S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 5-year retention.
Enable S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 5-year retention period.
q.k: nobody, not even root, can delete → Object Lock compliance mode
x: MFA Delete adds friction, but an authorized user with MFA can still delete versions.
An administrator can change the bucket policy.
Governance mode can be bypassed by users with s3:BypassGovernanceRetention.
In compliance mode no user, including root, can delete or overwrite a protected version or shorten the retention.

q: Users sometimes overwrite or delete important objects in an S3 bucket by mistake. The company wants to be able to recover previous versions.

q.k: recover from accidental overwrite or delete → versioning

Speeds up uploads.
Protects data at rest, not against deletion.
Lists objects; doesn't keep old versions.

q: A company must keep an automatic copy of every new object from a bucket in eu-west-1 in a bucket in eu-central-1, owned by a separate backup account, for disaster recovery.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Run AWS DataSync once a day.
Enable versioning on both buckets and configure S3 Cross-Region Replication to the bucket in the backup account, with ownership changed to the destination account.
Create a Lambda function triggered by every upload that copies the object.
q.k: automatic copy to another Region/account → Cross-Region Replication (needs versioning)
x: Not continuous, and more to manage.

Only speeds up uploads.
Works, but custom code to maintain for a built-in feature.

q.k: replicate existing objects → S3 Batch Replication
x: Rules only apply to new objects.
Unrelated to replication.
Batch Replication replicates existing objects, and objects that previously failed to replicate.
Versioning can't be turned off once enabled, only suspended, and that wouldn't help.

q: A company must encrypt S3 objects at rest with keys it controls, with an audit trail of every key use in CloudTrail and the ability to disable the key.
Which encryption option meets these requirements?
o: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
Client-side encryption with keys stored in the application
No encryption; S3 is private by default
q.k: control the key + audit key use → SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
x: S3 manages the keys; you can't control, disable, or audit individual key use.
Customer managed KMS keys give key policies, rotation, disabling, and CloudTrail logs of every use.
Puts key management in the application, with no central audit or control.

q: After enabling SSE-KMS on a bucket that receives millions of small objects per day, the company's AWS KMS request costs have increased sharply.

o: Use an AWS managed key instead of a customer managed key.
Enable S3 Bucket Keys for the bucket.
q.k: high KMS request cost with SSE-KMS → S3 Bucket Keys
x: Shifts the burden to the app and loses SSE-KMS.
Still calls KMS for each object.
A bucket-level key generates data keys locally for a period, cutting calls to KMS by up to 99%.
Violates the encryption requirement.

q: A web application lets users download private reports stored in S3. Each link must work only for the user who requested it and only for 15 minutes. The bucket must stay private.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Make the objects public and use obscure names.
Generate an S3 presigned URL with a 15-minute expiration from the application.
Add a bucket policy that allows all users for 15 minutes.
q.k: temporary access to a private object → presigned URL
x: Security through obscurity; anyone with the URL can download forever.
A presigned URL grants time-limited access to one object using the app's credentials, without changing bucket permissions.

Website hosting needs public access.

q: Users in Asia and South America upload large files (several GB) to an S3 bucket in us-east-1. Uploads are slow and sometimes fail.
Which TWO actions improve upload speed and reliability? (Select TWO.)
o: Change the storage class to S3 One Zone-IA.
q.k: distant users + large uploads → Transfer Acceleration + multipart upload
x: Routes uploads through the nearest CloudFront edge location over the AWS network.
Uploads parts in parallel and retries only failed parts. Recommended above 100 MB.
Unrelated to speed.
Unrelated to transfer speed.
Unrelated.

q: A company hosts a static website in a private S3 bucket and wants to serve it globally over HTTPS with a custom domain. Users must not be able to access the bucket directly.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Enable S3 static website hosting and make the bucket public.
Use an Amazon CloudFront distribution with the S3 bucket as origin, using origin access control (OAC), and a bucket policy that allows only the distribution.
Put an ALB in front of the bucket.
Use S3 presigned URLs for every page.
q.k: private bucket + global HTTPS + no direct access → CloudFront + OAC
x: Public bucket, and the S3 website endpoint doesn't support HTTPS directly.
OAC lets only CloudFront read the bucket. CloudFront provides HTTPS, caching, and a custom domain with an ACM certificate.
ALBs can't target S3 directly this way.
Impractical for a website.

q: Whenever a new object is uploaded to a bucket, three independent systems must be notified: a Lambda function, an SQS queue for batch processing, and an email alert.
Which design is MOST scalable and decoupled?
o: Configure S3 event notifications to send to Amazon EventBridge, and create rules that route the event to Lambda, SQS, and SNS (email).
Configure one S3 event notification to Lambda, which calls the other two.
Poll the bucket every minute from EC2.
q.k: many consumers of S3 events → EventBridge (or SNS fan-out)
x: EventBridge receives all S3 events and can route them to many targets with filtering. SNS fan-out to SQS and Lambda is an alternative.
Couples the systems and adds a failure point.
Polling is inefficient.
Inventory is a scheduled report.

q: An application needs block storage for a transactional database on EC2 that requires 40,000 consistent IOPS and sub-millisecond latency, with 99.999% durability.
Which EBS volume type should be used?
q.k: high, consistent IOPS + highest durability → io2 (Block Express)
x: gp3 is designed for 99.8–99.9% durability, not 99.999%, and isn't the choice for consistently high, latency-critical IOPS at this durability level.
Throughput-optimized HDD for sequential workloads; not for IOPS.
io2 offers 99.999% durability, high provisioned IOPS (well above 40,000), and sub-millisecond latency.
Cold HDD: lowest cost, lowest performance.

q: A company uses gp2 volumes. Some volumes are large only to get more IOPS, because gp2 IOPS scale with size.
How can the company reduce cost without lowering performance?
o: Migrate to gp3 volumes and provision IOPS and throughput independently of size.
q.k: gp2 oversized for IOPS → gp3 (IOPS and throughput independent of size, ~20% cheaper)
x: gp3 includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline at any size, with extra IOPS and throughput bought separately, and costs less per GB than gp2.
More expensive.
HDD; not suitable for random IOPS.
Ephemeral storage.

q: A big data job reads large log files sequentially from EBS. It needs high throughput at low cost; IOPS doesn't matter.
Which volume type is MOST cost-effective?
q.k: large sequential reads, throughput, cheap → st1
x: Paying for IOPS that aren't needed.
Fine, but more expensive per GB for large sequential datasets.
st1 is built for frequently accessed, throughput-intensive sequential workloads such as big data and log processing.
Cheapest, but for infrequently accessed data with lower throughput.

q: A company has an unencrypted EBS volume attached to a production instance and must encrypt it.
What is the correct procedure?

Create a snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, create a new volume from the encrypted snapshot, and swap it in.
Attach a KMS key to the instance.
Encrypt the file system with a Lambda function.
q.k: encrypt an existing unencrypted EBS volume → snapshot → encrypted copy → new volume
x: An existing volume can't be encrypted in place.
Copying a snapshot with encryption produces an encrypted snapshot, from which you create an encrypted volume.
Not how EBS encryption works.
Not a supported approach.

q: A security policy requires every new EBS volume in an account to be encrypted, even if developers forget to choose encryption.
What is the simplest way to enforce this?
o: Write a Lambda function that encrypts volumes after creation.
Enable EBS encryption by default in each Region of the account.
Use AWS Config to report unencrypted volumes.
q.k: all new volumes encrypted automatically → EBS encryption by default
x: Can't encrypt in place, and it's complex.
With encryption by default turned on, every new volume and snapshot copy in that Region is encrypted automatically.
Not a real fix and limits instance choice.
Detects but doesn't enforce.

q: An EBS volume is attached to an instance in AZ-a. The company needs to run the same data on a new instance in AZ-b.
How can it do this?
o: Detach the volume and attach it to the instance in AZ-b.
Create a snapshot of the volume and create a new volume from it in AZ-b.
q.k: EBS volumes are AZ-scoped → snapshot to move between AZs
x: A volume can only attach to instances in its own AZ.

Multi-Attach works only within the same AZ.
Unrelated to EBS.

q: Volumes restored from snapshots have high latency on first access because blocks are loaded lazily from S3. A database restored for DR must deliver full performance immediately.
Which feature should be used?
o: EBS Fast Snapshot Restore on the snapshot in the target AZ
q.k: full performance immediately after restore → Fast Snapshot Restore
x: FSR makes volumes created from the snapshot fully initialized at creation, with no first-read penalty.
Doesn't avoid lazy loading.
Shares a volume between instances; unrelated.

q: Dozens of Linux EC2 instances across three Availability Zones must read and write the same files concurrently through a POSIX file system. Storage must grow and shrink automatically.
Which service meets these requirements?
o: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
q.k: shared Linux file system across AZs, elastic → EFS
