EFS is a managed NFS file system, accessible concurrently from many instances across AZs, and it scales automatically.
SMB for Windows workloads.
Object storage, not a POSIX file system.

q: An EFS file system holds 10 TB of files. Most files aren't read after 30 days, but they must stay in the same file system.
How can the company reduce cost with the LEAST effort?
o: Move old files to S3 with a script.
Enable an EFS lifecycle policy to move files not accessed for 30 days to EFS Infrequent Access (or Archive).
Use EFS One Zone with no backups.
q.k: EFS cold files → lifecycle management to IA/Archive
x: Changes the path and adds code to maintain.
Lifecycle management moves files to the cheaper IA or Archive storage class transparently. Same path for the app.
EBS isn't shared and doesn't solve tiering.
Changes resilience, not access tiers, and risks data.

q: A company is moving Windows file shares to AWS. Users access them with SMB, and permissions are managed with Active Directory and NTFS ACLs. The company wants a fully managed service.
Which service should be used?
o: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon S3 with S3 File Gateway
q.k: SMB + AD + NTFS ACLs → FSx for Windows File Server
x: NFS for Linux.
High-performance file system for HPC, Linux clients.
Native Windows file system with SMB, AD integration, and NTFS permissions, fully managed.
File Gateway is for on-premises access to S3; it isn't a managed Windows file server.

q: A genomics workload processes a dataset stored in S3 with thousands of compute nodes. It needs a file system with hundreds of GB/s throughput and sub-millisecond latency, linked to the S3 bucket.
Which service meets these requirements?
o: Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Mount the bucket with an EBS volume
q.k: HPC/ML + extreme throughput + S3 data → FSx for Lustre
x: Lustre delivers very high throughput for HPC and integrates with S3, exposing objects as files and writing results back.
Scalable, but not at this performance level.
For Windows SMB workloads.

q: A company runs NetApp ONTAP on premises and serves the same data over NFS and SMB, using snapshots and SnapMirror. It wants a managed equivalent in AWS.
Which service should it choose?
q.k: ONTAP features, NFS + SMB multi-protocol → FSx for NetApp ONTAP
x: Fully managed ONTAP with multi-protocol access, snapshots, SnapMirror, and data efficiency.
NFS only, no ONTAP features.

q: A DynamoDB table holds critical financial data. The company needs to recover from accidental writes or deletes to any second within the last 35 days.
What should be enabled?
q.k: restore to any second in 35 days → DynamoDB PITR
x: Restores only to the time of each backup.
PITR enables continuous backups and restores to any second in the retention window (up to 35 days) into a new table.
Change stream; not a backup.
Replicates the mistakes to all Regions.

q: A DynamoDB table uses CustomerId as its partition key. The application now must query orders by Status across all customers efficiently.
What should be added?
o: A local secondary index on Status
A global secondary index with Status as its partition key
A scan with a filter expression
q.k: query by a different partition key → GSI
x: An LSI keeps the same partition key (CustomerId), and must be created with the table.
A GSI has its own partition and sort keys, so you can query by Status across the whole table. It can be added at any time.
Doesn't create a new access pattern.
A scan reads the whole table: slow and expensive.

q: A web application repeatedly runs the same expensive SQL queries against RDS. The team wants to reduce database load and improve response times by caching query results, with replication and automatic failover for the cache.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Amazon ElastiCache for Redis (Redis OSS or Valkey) with replication and Multi-AZ
q.k: cache + replication + automatic failover → ElastiCache Redis/Valkey
x: Memcached is simple and multithreaded, but has no replication, persistence, or failover.
Redis/Valkey supports replicas, Multi-AZ automatic failover, and persistence.
Expensive and doesn't avoid repeated work.
Caches HTTP responses at the edge, not database query results.

q: A game needs a real-time leaderboard that ranks millions of players by score and returns the top 100 instantly.
Which service and feature fit BEST?
o: Amazon RDS with ORDER BY on every request
q.k: leaderboard / ranking → Redis sorted sets
x: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score in memory, so rank and top-N queries are near-instant.
Expensive at this scale and latency.
Not for real-time ranking.
No sorted data structures.

q: A company wants to run complex analytical SQL queries over petabytes of structured sales data, joined with data that stays in S3, with columnar storage.
Which service should it use?
o: Amazon Redshift with Redshift Spectrum for the S3 data
q.k: data warehouse, petabytes, OLAP (+ S3 queries) → Redshift (+ Spectrum)
x: OLTP database; not built for petabyte analytics.
Key-value; no complex SQL analytics.
Redshift is a columnar MPP data warehouse. Spectrum queries data in S3 without loading it.
Cache.

q: A social network needs to query relationships such as 'friends of friends who like this product' across billions of connections with low latency.
Which database should be used?
q.k: highly connected relationships → graph DB (Neptune)
x: Neptune is a managed graph database (Gremlin, openCypher, SPARQL) built for relationship traversals.
Analytics warehouse; not graph traversals.
Recursive joins over billions of relationships are slow.
Time series.

q: A company runs MongoDB on self-managed EC2 instances and wants a fully managed, MongoDB-compatible document database with minimal application changes.
Which service should it use?
q.k: managed MongoDB-compatible → DocumentDB
x: Different API; requires rewriting data access.
DocumentDB is compatible with MongoDB APIs and drivers, fully managed.
Cassandra-compatible.
Graph.

q: A company runs Apache Cassandra on premises and wants a serverless, Cassandra-compatible (CQL) service on AWS.
Which service should it use?
q.k: Cassandra / CQL → Keyspaces
x: Keyspaces is serverless and works with CQL and existing Cassandra drivers.
MongoDB-compatible.
Relational.
Redis-compatible.

q: Thousands of IoT sensors send temperature readings every second. The company needs to store trillions of data points and run time-window queries with automatic tiering of older data.
Which database fits BEST?
q.k: time series at scale → Timestream
x: Timestream is purpose-built for time series, with built-in time functions and tiering from memory to magnetic storage.
Doesn't scale well for trillions of time series points.
Graph.
Document store.

q: An application needs a Redis-compatible database that is the primary, durable data store, with microsecond reads and data durability across multiple AZs through a transaction log.
Which service meets these requirements?
q.k: Redis-compatible primary database, durable → MemoryDB
x: A cache, not built as a durable primary store.
MemoryDB is Redis/Valkey-compatible with a Multi-AZ transactional log for durability, so it can be the primary database.
Not Redis-compatible.
Relational, not microsecond in-memory.

q: A company must migrate an on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL with minimal downtime. The schema, stored procedures, and code objects must be converted.
Which combination of services should be used?
o: AWS Schema Conversion Tool (or DMS Schema Conversion) for the schema, and AWS DMS with full load plus change data capture (CDC) for the data
q.k: heterogeneous migration with minimal downtime → SCT + DMS (full load + CDC)
x: File transfer tools; no schema conversion or replication.
SCT converts the schema and code between engines. DMS copies existing data and then replicates ongoing changes, so the cutover is short.
Not database migration tools.
For PostgreSQL to PostgreSQL, not Oracle.

q: An RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ instance fails over to the standby. What do applications need to do to reconnect?
o: Update their connection strings to the standby's IP address.
Nothing beyond reconnecting; the DNS endpoint is updated to point to the new primary.
q.k: Multi-AZ failover → same endpoint, DNS flips
x: The endpoint stays the same.
RDS updates the DNS record of the endpoint. Apps should handle reconnection and avoid caching DNS for long.
Not needed for Multi-AZ.
Not needed.

q: A company needs an RDS deployment that provides automatic failover in under about 35 seconds and also allows read traffic on the standby instances.
Which deployment option should it choose?
o: Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment (two readable standbys)
q.k: faster failover + readable standbys in RDS → Multi-AZ DB cluster
x: No automatic failover.
The single standby isn't readable, and failover is slower.
A Multi-AZ DB cluster has a writer and two readable standbys in different AZs with faster failover.
For OS and database customization, not this requirement.

q: A development team needs a full copy of a 5 TB Aurora production database for testing, created in minutes, without doubling storage costs immediately.
Which feature should be used?
o: Create a read replica and promote it
q.k: fast, space-efficient copy of Aurora → cloning (copy-on-write)
x: Takes longer and copies all the data.
Cloning uses copy-on-write: the clone shares pages with the source until they change, so it's fast and cheap.
Takes time and copies data in full.
Slow and full copy.

q: A cross-Region RDS for MySQL read replica exists in eu-west-1 for DR. The primary Region fails.
What must be done to make the replica accept writes?
o: Promote the read replica to a standalone instance and point the application to it.
q.k: cross-Region replica for DR → promote (manual)
x: Replicas are read-only.
Promotion turns the replica into an independent, writable instance. Replication stops.
Doesn't make it writable.
Unnecessary; the replica already has more recent data.

q: An application needs full-text search, fuzzy matching, and log analytics with dashboards over data stored in DynamoDB.
Which service should be added?
o: Amazon OpenSearch Service, fed from DynamoDB (for example via zero-ETL integration or Streams)
q.k: full-text search / log analytics → OpenSearch
x: OpenSearch provides full-text search, fuzzy queries, and dashboards; data can flow from DynamoDB automatically.
SQL analytics, not search.
SQL on S3, not full-text search.
Cache; no search.

q: A DynamoDB table has steady, predictable traffic of about 2,000 writes per second all day. It currently uses on-demand capacity.
How can the company reduce cost?
o: Switch to provisioned capacity with auto scaling (and consider reserved capacity).
q.k: steady predictable traffic → provisioned (+ reserved) is cheaper than on-demand
x: For steady workloads provisioned capacity costs less than on-demand, and reserved capacity cuts it further.
Helps reads, not writes, and adds cost.
Adds cost.
Doesn't affect write throughput cost.

q: A database on RDS must not be reachable from the internet. Only the application servers in private subnets should connect on port 5432.
Which configuration meets these requirements?
o: Set Publicly Accessible to Yes and use a strong password.
Place the DB instance in private subnets (DB subnet group), set Publicly Accessible to No, and allow port 5432 only from the application security group.
Use a NACL that allows 0.0.0.0/0 on 5432.
Place the database in a public subnet with an Elastic IP.
q.k: private DB → private subnets + not public + SG referencing app SG
x: Exposes the database to the internet.
Private subnets, no public endpoint, and a security group that only accepts the app tier.
Opens it to everyone.
Exposes the database.

q: A company's Aurora MySQL developers sometimes run bad UPDATE statements. They want to rewind the database to a point a few minutes earlier in seconds, without restoring to a new cluster.
Which feature meets this requirement?
q.k: rewind in place quickly (Aurora MySQL) → Backtrack
x: Backtrack rewinds the same cluster to an earlier time without restoring from backup.
Creates a new cluster and takes longer.
Cross-Region replication.
Creates a copy; doesn't undo changes in place.

q: A company wants to analyze recent transactional data from Aurora in Amazon Redshift within seconds, without building and maintaining ETL pipelines.
Which feature should be used?
o: Aurora zero-ETL integration with Amazon Redshift
q.k: near real-time analytics without ETL → zero-ETL integration
x: Pipelines to build and maintain, with lag.
Zero-ETL replicates data from Aurora to Redshift within seconds, managed by AWS.
Slow and manual.
Batch with lag.

q: A company runs a dev/test RDS database used only from 09:00 to 18:00 on weekdays.
How can it lower cost with the LEAST effort?
o: Delete and recreate it each day from a snapshot.
Stop the instance outside working hours with a scheduled automation (for example, EventBridge Scheduler or Instance Scheduler).
q.k: intermittent use → stop when idle (scheduled)
x: Works, but more effort and risk.
A stopped RDS instance doesn't incur instance-hour charges (storage is still billed). Note RDS restarts it after 7 days.
Doubles cost.
Pays for 24/7 regardless of use.

q: Hundreds of short-lived Lambda invocations connect to Aurora PostgreSQL, opening and closing connections constantly. The database CPU is high because of connection overhead, and failovers cause many errors.
Which solution improves this?
o: Add Amazon RDS Proxy to pool connections and reduce failover impact.
q.k: connection churn from serverless + faster failover → RDS Proxy
x: Addresses the symptom at higher cost.
RDS Proxy pools and reuses connections, and keeps client connections open during failover, reducing failover time.
A large migration not required by the problem.
Removes resilience.

q: A production RDS for PostgreSQL instance runs 24/7 with steady load and will be used for at least 3 years.
How can the company reduce its cost the MOST?
o: Buy RDS Reserved Instances for the instance class (3-year term).
q.k: steady 24/7 RDS → RDS Reserved Instances
x: RDS RIs give a large discount for steady usage.
It's production and used 24/7.
Serverless suits variable load; for steady load it's usually more expensive.
Compute Savings Plans don't cover RDS.

q: An RDS for MySQL instance is consistently at 10% CPU and 20% memory, on a db.r6g.4xlarge.
What should be done?
o: Right-size to a smaller instance class during a maintenance window.
q.k: low utilization → right-size
x: A smaller class halves or quarters cost; check with Performance Insights first.
Adds cost.
Adds cost (unless HA is needed for other reasons).
Unrelated.

q: An application needs its RDS database to survive a full Region outage with an RPO of minutes and an RTO under 1 hour, at moderate cost. It uses RDS for PostgreSQL (not Aurora).
Which solution fits BEST?
o: A cross-Region read replica, promoted during a disaster
Daily automated snapshots in the same Region
Two instances in the same AZ
q.k: RDS cross-Region DR with low RPO → cross-Region read replica
x: Asynchronous replication gives an RPO of minutes; promotion takes minutes.
Protects only against AZ failure.
Same-Region snapshots don't survive a Region outage, and RPO is a day.
No resilience.

q: A company must keep RDS backups for 7 years for compliance. Automated backups only allow 35 days of retention.
How can this be done with the least effort?
o: Use AWS Backup with a plan that creates snapshots and retains them for 7 years (optionally copying them to another account or Region).
Increase automated backup retention to 7 years.
Export the database to CSV monthly.
Keep a read replica for 7 years.
q.k: long-term RDS retention → AWS Backup (manual snapshots)
x: Backup plans create snapshots on a schedule with long retention.
35 days is the maximum.
Manual and hard to restore.
Not a backup.

q: A DynamoDB table stores 5 TB of order history. Only the last 90 days are queried frequently; older data is read a few times a year.
How can storage costs be reduced while keeping data in DynamoDB?
o: Change the table class to DynamoDB Standard-Infrequent Access (or move old items to a Standard-IA table).
q.k: DynamoDB storage-heavy, rarely read → Standard-IA table class
x: Standard-IA lowers storage price (higher per-request cost) for tables dominated by storage.
Speeds reads; adds cost.
Changes throughput billing, not storage.
Adds cost.

q: Old DynamoDB items must be kept for analytics in S3 and removed from the table automatically.
Which approach has the LEAST operational overhead?
o: Set TTL on the items and process TTL deletions from DynamoDB Streams with Lambda (or Firehose) to write them to S3.
Run a nightly scan and copy job.
q.k: expire + archive → TTL + Streams to S3
x: TTL deletes for free; the stream records the deleted items so they can be archived.
Consumes capacity and needs maintenance.
Unrelated.
Unrelated.

q: Write traffic on a DynamoDB table is concentrated on a few partition key values (for example, today's date), causing throttling even though total capacity is high.
What is the best fix?
o: Choose a higher-cardinality partition key or add a random/calculated suffix (write sharding).
Add a GSI on the same key.
q.k: hot partition → better key distribution
x: Spreading writes over many key values distributes load across partitions.
Inherits the same hot key.
DAX caches reads, not writes.
Unrelated to writes.

q: An application reads a DynamoDB item immediately after writing it and sometimes gets the old value.
What should the application do if it must always see the latest data?
o: Use strongly consistent reads (ConsistentRead=true) on the base table.
q.k: read-after-write freshness → strongly consistent read
x: Strongly consistent reads return the latest committed write (they cost 2x eventually consistent reads and aren't available on GSIs).
GSIs are eventually consistent.
Item cache can return stale data.
Unrelated.

q: An ElastiCache for Redis cluster used for user sessions runs on a single node. When the node failed, all users were logged out.
How should it be configured?
o: Enable replicas with Multi-AZ and automatic failover.
q.k: cache HA → replicas + Multi-AZ automatic failover
x: A replica in another AZ is promoted automatically if the primary fails.
No replication at all.
Still a single point of failure.
Makes data loss worse.

q: A reporting query on Aurora PostgreSQL competes with the OLTP workload. The reports need dedicated replicas with larger instance types than other replicas.
How should the team route report traffic?
o: Create an Aurora custom endpoint that includes only the large replicas, and point the reporting tool at it.
Create a read replica in another Region.
q.k: route a workload to specific replicas → Aurora custom endpoint
x: Custom endpoints group chosen instances, so reports hit only the large replicas.
Goes to the writer.
Spreads across all replicas, mixing workloads.
Adds latency and cost.

q: A company runs a SQL Server database on RDS and pays for licenses included in the hourly price. It owns no SQL Server licenses. The workload could run on PostgreSQL with modest code changes.
What reduces licensing cost the MOST over time?
o: Migrate to Aurora PostgreSQL (or RDS for PostgreSQL) using DMS and Schema Conversion.
Move to a larger SQL Server instance.
q.k: commercial engine license cost → migrate to open-source engine
x: Open-source engines carry no license fee; DMS and SCT handle the migration.
More expensive.
Only useful with your own licenses.
Adds cost.

q: A Redshift cluster is busy only during month-end reporting and idle the rest of the month.
Which option is MOST cost-effective?
o: Amazon Redshift Serverless (pay for compute used) or pausing a provisioned cluster when idle
q.k: intermittent warehouse usage → Redshift Serverless or pause/resume
x: Serverless bills only while queries run; a provisioned cluster can be paused to stop compute charges.
Pays for idle capacity.
More expensive.
Not built for warehouse analytics.

q: An online retailer runs its order database on Amazon RDS for MySQL in a Single-AZ deployment. Last month a hardware failure caused 40 minutes of downtime and lost 5 minutes of orders. The business now requires automatic failover in under 2 minutes with no data loss, and reporting queries that currently slow down checkout must be moved off the primary.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Create two read replicas in other AZs and promote one if the primary fails.
Convert to a Multi-AZ DB cluster deployment (one writer and two readable standbys) and point reporting at the reader endpoint.
Take snapshots every 5 minutes and restore on failure.
Move the database to a larger instance type.
q.k: no data loss + fast automatic failover + offload reads → Multi-AZ DB cluster (readable standbys)
x: Asynchronous replication can lose data, and promotion isn't automatic.
Semi-synchronous replication avoids data loss, failover typically completes in under a minute, and the standbys serve reads.
Restores take long and lose data.
Doesn't add HA.

q: A ticketing platform uses DynamoDB. When popular events go on sale, traffic jumps from 500 to 80,000 reads per second within a minute, mostly for the same few event items, and users see throttling and high latency.
Which solution handles these spikes with the LEAST code change?
o: Switch the table to on-demand mode and add DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for the hot event items.
Add a GSI on the event ID.
Move the data to RDS with read replicas.
q.k: sudden spikes + hot keys on reads → on-demand + DAX
x: On-demand absorbs sudden traffic, and DAX serves repeated reads of hot items from memory with the DynamoDB API.
Pays for peak all the time and still suffers from hot partitions.
Same hot key in the index.
A big rewrite and doesn't solve spikes.

q: A global SaaS company uses Aurora PostgreSQL in eu-west-1. It needs to serve low-latency reads to users in North America, and in a regional disaster it must be able to resume writes in us-east-1 within minutes with at most a few seconds of data loss.
Which solution meets these requirements?
o: Cross-Region read replica of RDS for PostgreSQL
Aurora Global Database with a secondary cluster in us-east-1, using managed failover (or detach and promote) in a disaster
DMS continuous replication to an RDS instance in us-east-1
q.k: Aurora + cross-Region reads + RPO seconds/RTO minutes → Global Database
x: That's for RDS, not Aurora, and has higher lag and slower promotion.
Storage-level replication under ~1 s, local reads in us-east-1, promotion in minutes.
RPO of a day.
More to manage and slower failover.

q: A serverless API on Lambda queries Aurora MySQL. During traffic spikes, the database reaches its maximum connections and returns errors, while CPU usage stays low. A failover last week also caused 30 seconds of errors.
Which solution addresses both issues?
o: Place Amazon RDS Proxy between Lambda and Aurora.
q.k: connection exhaustion from Lambda + failover impact → RDS Proxy
x: Raises the connection limit slightly but doesn't fix connection churn.
RDS Proxy pools connections and keeps client connections open during failover, cutting errors and failover time.
Writes and connections still hit the writer.
Unrelated.

q: A mobile app stores user profiles in DynamoDB with userId as the partition key. A new feature must list all users in a given country sorted by signup date, and another must look up users by email address.
What should be added to the table?
o: Two global secondary indexes: one with country as partition key and signupDate as sort key, and one with email as partition key
q.k: new access patterns with different keys → GSIs
x: GSIs support queries on any attribute and can be added to an existing table.
LSIs keep the userId partition key and must be created with the table.
Scans read the whole table.
A cache, not an index.

q: A company runs an internal reporting database on RDS for PostgreSQL (db.r6g.2xlarge, Multi-AZ). It's used only during office hours on weekdays, and a 10-minute delay to start each morning is acceptable. Downtime outside office hours is acceptable.
Which TWO actions reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
o: Stop the instance outside office hours with a scheduled automation, restarting it before work.
Turn off Multi-AZ, since standby availability isn't needed for this internal workload.
q.k: part-time internal DB → stop when idle + drop unneeded HA
x: Stopped instances don't pay instance hours (storage still billed).
Multi-AZ doubles instance cost; downtime is acceptable here.
Paying 24/7 for a part-time workload is wasteful.
Adds cost.
More expensive storage.

q: A company migrates a 3 TB on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL. The application can be down for at most 15 minutes during cutover. The database is constantly being written to.
Which approach meets the downtime requirement?
o: Export with Oracle Data Pump, copy to S3, and import into Aurora during a weekend.
Convert the schema with AWS Schema Conversion Tool (or DMS Schema Conversion), then use AWS DMS with a full load plus ongoing change data capture, and cut over once replication catches up.
Use AWS Snowball to ship the data files.
q.k: heterogeneous + minimal downtime → SCT + DMS full load + CDC
x: Downtime equals the whole export and import time.
CDC keeps Aurora in sync while the source stays online; cutover takes minutes.
Offline transfer can't keep up with constant writes.
Not a database migration tool.

q: A gaming leaderboard needs to update scores for 5 million players and return a player's rank and the top 100 in under 10 ms. Scores must survive node failures without manual intervention.
Which solution fits BEST?
o: DynamoDB with a GSI on score
ElastiCache for Redis OSS (or Valkey) with sorted sets, cluster mode, replicas and Multi-AZ automatic failover
RDS for MySQL with an index on score
q.k: real-time ranking + HA → Redis sorted sets + replicas/Multi-AZ
x: Can't compute ranks efficiently.
Sorted sets give O(log N) ranking and top-N reads; replicas with automatic failover protect against node loss.
ORDER BY across millions of rows on every request is slow.
Analytics warehouse.

q: A DynamoDB table stores financial transactions. A buggy deployment overwrote thousands of items 3 hours ago. The company needs to restore the correct data with minimal data loss, and the table must stay online for new writes.
What should the team do?
o: Use point-in-time recovery to restore the table to a new table at a time just before the bad deployment, then copy the affected items back to the live table.
Restore the latest on-demand backup over the live table.
Disable the table and rebuild it from logs.
Use DynamoDB Streams to replay all events since table creation.
q.k: undo bad writes, keep table online → PITR to a new table + selective copy-back
x: PITR restores to any second into a new table, so the live table keeps working while you fix only the affected items.
On-demand backups can't overwrite the live table and may be older.
Causes downtime.
Streams retain only 24 hours.

q: An analytics team runs heavy SQL joins over 50 TB of historical sales data stored as Parquet in S3, plus 2 TB of recent data in a Redshift cluster. They want to query both together without loading the S3 data into Redshift.
Which solution meets this requirement?
o: Redshift Spectrum with an external schema in the Glue Data Catalog
q.k: join warehouse tables with S3 data in place → Redshift Spectrum
x: Spectrum queries S3 data through external tables and joins it with local Redshift tables.
Athena can't directly join tables stored inside the Redshift cluster this way.
Not an analytics engine.
Not built for this volume of analytics.

q: An order service sends orders directly to a fulfillment service over HTTP. When the fulfillment service is slow or down, orders are lost.
Which change decouples the services and prevents order loss?
o: Put an Application Load Balancer in front of the fulfillment service.
Have the order service send messages to an Amazon SQS queue, and have the fulfillment service poll the queue.
Increase the fulfillment service's instance size.
q.k: producer faster than consumer / consumer down → SQS queue between them
x: Still synchronous: if the backend is down, requests fail.
The queue durably stores messages until the consumer processes them, absorbing spikes and outages.
Doesn't solve outages.
DNS failover doesn't buffer requests.

q: A payment system must process messages exactly once and in the exact order they were sent for each customer account.
Which queue type should be used?
o: SQS FIFO queue using the account ID as the message group ID
q.k: order + exactly-once processing → SQS FIFO (message group per entity)
x: At-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering.
FIFO queues preserve order within a message group and deduplicate messages. Using the account ID as group lets different accounts process in parallel.
Standard SNS doesn't guarantee order.
A delivery stream to storage, not a work queue.

q: Consumers of an SQS queue take up to 4 minutes to process a message. Messages are sometimes processed twice because they reappear in the queue while still being processed.
What should be changed?
o: Increase the queue's visibility timeout to longer than the maximum processing time.
q.k: messages reappear during processing → visibility timeout too short
x: Retention is how long unprocessed messages are kept.
While a message is invisible, other consumers can't receive it. If processing outlasts the timeout, it reappears. Set it above max processing time (or extend it from the consumer).
Reduces empty receives, not duplicates.
Delays initial delivery only.

q: Some malformed messages fail processing repeatedly and block a queue's consumers, while good messages are delayed.
How should this be handled?
o: Delete the queue and recreate it.
Configure a dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount, so failing messages move aside for later analysis.
Increase the visibility timeout to 12 hours.
q.k: poison messages → dead-letter queue
x: Loses all messages.
After the maximum number of receives, SQS moves the message to the DLQ so the main queue keeps flowing. You can redrive later.
Delays the problem without solving it.
Doesn't solve failing messages.

q: Consumers poll an SQS queue constantly. Most ReceiveMessage calls return empty, generating cost and CPU usage.
What should be changed?
o: Enable long polling by setting ReceiveMessageWaitTimeSeconds up to 20 seconds.
q.k: many empty receives → long polling
x: Long polling waits for messages to arrive before responding, reducing empty responses and cost.
Unrelated.
Unrelated to empty receives.
Makes it worse.

q: Workers on EC2 in an Auto Scaling group process messages from an SQS queue. The backlog sometimes grows to hours. The company wants the group to scale based on how much work is waiting.
Which scaling approach is BEST?
o: Target tracking on average CPU utilization
Target tracking on a custom metric of backlog per instance (ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible divided by running instances)
q.k: queue workers → scale on backlog per instance
x: CPU doesn't reflect how many messages are waiting.
Backlog per instance measures how many messages each worker must handle, and target tracking keeps it at an acceptable level.
Ignores actual backlog.
Unrelated to queue depth.

q: When a new user signs up, four independent services (email, analytics, CRM, rewards) must each receive the event and process it at their own pace. Each must get every event even if it is temporarily down.
Which architecture meets these requirements?
o: Publish to an SNS topic with four SQS queues subscribed (fan-out).
Send the event to one SQS queue read by all four services.
Write the event to an S3 bucket.
q.k: one event → many independent durable consumers → SNS + SQS fan-out
x: SNS delivers a copy to each queue; each service reads its own queue, so outages don't lose events.
With one queue, each message goes to only one consumer.
Tight coupling; one failure breaks the signup.
Not an event distribution mechanism.

q: An SNS topic publishes all order events. The shipping queue should receive only events where country is 'ES' or 'PT'.
How can this be done without changing the publisher?
o: Create a separate topic per country.
Add a subscription filter policy on the shipping queue's subscription.
Filter in the consumer and discard others.
q.k: subscriber only gets matching messages → SNS filter policy
x: Changes the publisher.
Filter policies on message attributes or body deliver only matching messages to that subscriber.
Works, but wastes processing and cost.
Unrelated to filtering.

q: A company wants to react to events from AWS services, from its own applications, and from SaaS partners (such as Zendesk), routing them with content-based rules to Lambda, Step Functions, and SQS.
Which service fits BEST?
q.k: event bus with rules, SaaS partners, AWS events → EventBridge
x: Pub/sub, but no SaaS partner integrations and simpler filtering.
EventBridge receives AWS, custom, and partner events, and routes them with rich pattern matching to many targets.
A data stream for high-throughput ordered records.
Managed broker for ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ.

q: A company wants to run a Lambda function every day at 02:00 UTC without managing any servers.
What is the simplest solution?
o: A cron job on an EC2 instance
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler (or a scheduled EventBridge rule) targeting the Lambda function
A Step Functions wait state running forever
q.k: serverless cron → EventBridge Scheduler
x: A server to run and pay for.
EventBridge Scheduler supports cron and rate expressions with time zones and invokes the function directly.
Maximum delay is 15 minutes.
Wasteful and awkward.

q: After a bug in a consumer, a company needs to reprocess the events that EventBridge delivered over the last 3 days.
What should it have configured?
o: An EventBridge archive on the event bus, then replay the events
